text: The Operating Systems course was necessary for my track, and the grading felt transparent enough in how assignments mapped to the rubric, even if some instructions left too much room for interpretation. TAs were responsive and gave practical tips, though feedback varied a lot by assignment and sometimes came a bit late. I did mostly solo work, but the real value came from the hands-on lab with the kernel module patch; it wasn’t perfect, but it taught me a lot even as I struggled to stay motivated some weeks.

I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics, so this course felt like a bumpy start. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and I did okay when I could focus, but I struggled most of the term and barely passed, which was frustrating because I had time but motivation fluctuated. The grading rubrics felt vague, and feedback came sparse until it was almost too late, which didn’t help when I needed to correct course for the next assignment. The platform would throw quirks that stressed me out more than the content, like random submission hiccups right around deadlines, and there weren’t many assessments, but each one mattered a lot. Still, the occasional project on a small database model helped me see where I was headed, even if I wouldn’t take the course again.

Tilling through the lectures with a full-time job was rough, but Dr. Park’s big-picture explanations helped me grasp concepts even if the examples felt thin. The peer discussions saved a lot, though the grading rubric felt vague and the prerequisite assumptions were tougher than I expected.

Linear Algebra fit into my evenings around another hard class, which made the mid-program core feel heavier than it probably is on paper. I kept up with almost every lecture, but the tooling setup was a constant drag—getting the IDE and the math package to play nicely ate into study time more than I’d like to admit. The assessment mix never quite lined up with the lectures, and I watched the grading comments land late, which left me chasing what I’d missed for days. Office hours were a relief—the professor could actually walk through a matrix decomposition and explain where I was tripping up, even if the overall pacing felt off. There was a small project with a stubborn deadline pattern that stood out in my memory, but I don’t want to overfit on one moment.

In Calculus II with Dr. Park, I used the materials selectively and balanced it with other demanding courses; exams felt fair enough, but the timing on feedback dragged, and the forums could be supportive yet dismissive at times, especially when I struggled with a deadline glitch.

I had enough time to slog through the summer term, but the pace felt compressed and uneven, which made the practical parts feel more frustrating than they should have been. I’m a coder with strong hands-on skills but weak theory, and this course didn’t quite bridge the gaps the way I hoped; the material would sometimes click, then drift into abstract edge cases that didn’t map to what I actually need for a project. The weekly labs and the project were where the friction showed up most: setting up the tooling was a hassle, and I spent more time fighting environment quirks than actually debugging the network flows we were meant to test. Our help channel felt more about peers trading quick notes than getting solid guidance from staff, which left me leaning on a couple classmates who were similarly in the trenches. There were moments when I learned a lot, especially around basic routing concepts, but the overall experience was marred by uneven teaching week to week and an exam format that didn’t feel fair given how scattered the pacing was. In the end, I’d say it fills gaps better than expected on prerequisites, but the practical payoff and fairness of evaluation left me mostly disappointed.

I’m glad I stuck with Linear Algebra for my degree, even though I’m new to the basics and juggling a full-time job. Prof. Rios lectures can feel uneven week to week, but office hours rescue the course, and peer discussions usually save the day.

I took Database Systems in my last semester, juggling it with another hard class, and I genuinely went in curious about how the pieces fit, not just to check a box. The course felt like an advanced elective that moved at its own pace, with week-to-week delivery that could be uneven—one lecture would click and the next would feel rushed or vague, which made it hard to stay on top. Most of the work was solo, and while I didn’t rely on peers much, when I did, it was mostly informal help from classmates rather than staff pointers, which left me hovering between grasping a concept and staring at a confusing diagram for a while. Attendance patterns were a mess for me: I fell behind early and then clawed my way back around deadlines, which didn’t help the momentum. There were only a few assessments, but each carried a lot of weight, so a small misunderstanding could snowball. A concrete memory: the midterm required wiring together a normalization plan for a pretend database, and I swear I spent more time chasing ambiguous instructions than actually applying theory. I can’t honestly recommend it, despite some value.

Dr. Singh’s Computer Networks started off engaging, but I barely scraped by after midterm week; the mix of lectures didn’t quite line up with the assessments, and the grading rubric felt too vague. The peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and I found the prerequisite content surprisingly more helpful than expected.

I came into Operating Systems with a decent coding background but weaker theory, and it showed—the lectures felt accessible enough, but the prerequisite gap kept nagging me, especially since the workload was heavy on assignments with tight deadlines. The TAs were responsive and practical, which helped when I got stuck trying to get the toolchain set up, though that setup felt like a hurdle with little payoff for the effort. I started the term engaged and attended fairly often, but midsemester I slipped into juggling five deadlines at once and attendance faded as confusion telegraphed into projects. The turning point, around the late-semester midterm, left me feeling more confused than reassured about what I’d actually learned, and I’m left with mixed feelings about the overall value of the course for my track.

Calculus II felt like it fit into my schedule more than my curiosity, especially since I was juggling another hard class at the same time. Dr. Miller’s lectures are useful to rewatch, but they come off as dry and a bit thin on explanations, so I often left the recordings with more questions than answers. The peer discussions were the only real lifelines for me; talking through an integration by parts hiccup helped more than the official materials ever did. The course is clearly an advanced elective, and it works best if you already know some adjacent material, otherwise the leaps left me chasing notes and deadlines. I did fall behind at one point, then somehow caught up around a big deadline, which was a stressful pattern I kept repeating. The assessments felt fair in how they tested understanding, but the pace is exhausting, and the fast feedback on scores didn’t always clarify what I still didn’t get. I’d only recommend it if you come in prepared and ready to put in extra time, maybe with a study buddy, because the memory anchor of that early confusion shaped the rest of the term.

Midway through a brutal heavy semester, I’m slogging through Computer Networks mostly because it’s required for the degree, and I’ve treated it as my main focus that term. The lectures make the big ideas click pretty well, but the examples feel thin, so I’m often left building intuition on my own with the slides and a lot of “how does this apply to real traffic?” My worst bottleneck is the software stack—rough at first, a bit steadier after that initial scramble—but I can manage it, and the office hours are where the course suddenly saves itself, like last week when the TA walked me through a packet-trace issue I’d been spinning on for hours. The prerequisites line up okay, and I can see the thread, but the pace still leaves me racing time during the week, even with a single major project and a few quick quizzes.

As a returning student trying to shake off the rust, I found Data Structures useful for industry work but the notes and slides felt serviceable, not memorable, with sparse feedback until it was almost too late; the one big mismatch was grading, which hit harder since each assessment mattered a lot.

I took Database Systems in the summer term, and the pacing felt tight but oddly worked for my stronger coding background, even though the theory bits left me unsure about the deeper concepts. The grading rubric was vague and the report-heavy workload wore me down, but it filled in some prerequisite gaps better than I expected. I remember a quick office-hours chat where the TA walked through a messy query plan and it finally clicked, giving me enough confidence to push through the last deadline.

Took Data Structures in my first semester just to tick a specialization box, and wow the tooling setup alone felt endless; deadlines got brutal when the environment misbehaved, and the rapid-score feedback was blunt, but somehow the content helped me understand concepts I was shaky on, even if I’d still hesitate to take it again.

I took the Machine Learning intro course this semester, and I did it mostly to satisfy a genuine curiosity while trying to fit short evening sessions around a crazy heavy load. The lectures were clear and the pacing felt doable if I skipped a few late-night snack breaks, but the thing that sticks with me is how the grading felt opaque—like I could see the rubric in the syllabus, yet the actual feedback and the way points were awarded could shift without notice, which left me chasing the hidden rules instead of learning. I appreciated that the LMS flow and submission process were smooth enough to not add another hurdle, and I mostly worked solo anyway since the collaboration bit was minimal; I didn’t feel much peer pressure, just a quiet solo grind. When I emailed support about a deadline hiccup, the response came slow and I ended up scrambling to adjust my plan, which didn’t help my stress levels mid-semester. Still, I learned a lot, especially compared to my easier prerequisite, even if I disliked how the experience dragged at times and left me frustrated between bursts of interest. I’d still say I’d recommend broadly, just not to count on transparent grading or speedy email fixes.

I’m in my first semester in the program, juggling Linear Algebra with a couple of other demanding courses and a full-time job, so I came in feeling decent about proofs but less confident with systems-type work. Recorded lectures are a lifeline when I’m slammed, but they’re pretty dry, and I mostly skim notes rather than binge-listen. The quick feedback helped me adjust, but the overall assessment mix didn’t quite line up with what we covered in lectures, which left me chasing a few surprises on the tests. The platform quirks—things like the weird auto-save hiccup right before I was submitting—added unnecessary stress, and I found comparing this to the prerequisites I aced before only reinforced that it wasn’t going to be easy despite a sense of usefulness. I wouldn’t say I enjoyed it, but there were moments I realized the core ideas could be handy down the line.

Linear Algebra started accessible enough, but I’m a returning student who feels rusty, balancing this as one of several demanding courses. The software stack was rough at first—lots of canvas-like dashboards and weird plotting quirks—but it settled into something workable after the first couple of weeks. The group work sometimes adds value when everyone shows up with ideas, yet it flares with friction when parts aren’t aligned and I’m stuck doing extra legwork. The grading rubric always felt vague, and I barely passed after struggling most of the term; the prerequisite ramp-up is sharp, and I felt behind early on. I remember one hour in office hours where the TA explained a concept with a single intuitive example that finally clicked, but I’m not sure I’d recommend it without strong time management.

I took Cyber Security Basics mid-program and came away with a solid A after the curve, but the ride honestly felt up and down. Prof. Haddad runs a lot of big, time-intensive reports, and the pacing mid-semester hit a crunch that made the whole thing feel like a sprint to two deadlines in a row, which didn’t help my attendance slip as the weeks wore on. The lectures themselves sometimes felt uneven week to week, with the Friday recap not quite catching the messy details from Monday’s class, so I ended up relying on the forums, where people were helpful but occasionally dismissive when I asked basic setup questions. The tool setup was a slog—lots of environment bootstrapping and dependency juggling that didn’t translate into clearer learning payoff, which made the actual writing-heavy assessment feel heavier than it should have been. There was one big project that pushed a lot of time in a single week, and while the rubric was fair, I still finished exhausted and wondering if the effort matched the grade. Overall, the course gave me legitimate foundations but left me juggling a lot of logistics without much lighter path through the deeper material.

Taking Computer Networks with Dr. Park in my last semester was a mixed ride: I’m comfortable with proofs, but the systems side dragged me, especially since the collaboration structure mattered more than the official materials. The peer discussions helped a lot for grasping concepts, but the instructions left too much interpretation and the grading comments were detailed yet annoying in their delay, given I was juggling full-time work.

I’m not sure I’d recommend it, but Park is solid and I liked him, even as the grading felt harsh. The weeks dragged with tool glitches and sparse feedback, and the project-heavy setup plus high-stakes exams wore me down.

Took Computer Networks as a new-to-discipline student, and I started off engaged but my attendance faded mid-semester as deadlines piled up. Prof. Haddad’s class is heavy on assignments with tight turns, and instructions leave a lot up to interpretation, which didn’t help when feedback was sparse until after the next deadline. The forums helped at times, even if some replies felt a bit dismissive, and I’ll still recommend the course broadly to others starting out, since those turning-point moments stuck with me.

Cyber Security Basics was the main focus that term for me, since I was juggling a full-time job and only had a few dedicated study hours each week. The course really pushed the difficulty in a way that felt earned—projects were heavy, and the high-stakes exams kept a steady pressure that forced me to stay on top of deadlines, even when a mid-semester crunch made me fall behind for a bit. The lecturer knew the material and explained it clearly most days, but I did notice the feedback pacing varied a lot by assignment, which didn’t help when I needed to course-correct fast. Early on the software stack felt rough to get comfortable with, though it smoothed out once I got the hang of the tooling, which helped once I finally mapped out a workable workflow for a mixed environment of tools on the project. The course assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, so I spent extra time filling gaps, especially around threat modeling concepts you’d expect in a core mid-program course. Overall, it was solidly designed and the project-heavy assessment kept the energy up, even if one or two feedback rounds didn’t quite land for me.

Starting with a complaint: I kept feeling like the workload was set to stretch me, but oddly it paid off since I’m juggling a full-time job and still managed to keep up. Prof. Alvarez lectures are solid but not memorable; the real help came from my classmates, we bonded over debugging oddities in the ML project, and the stack felt rough at first but got smoother after a week. I earned a solid B that matched the effort, and the peer discussions became the main driver for understanding.

Machine Learning in mid-program already felt rough, especially since I had to fit study around short evening sessions and a heavy semester. The lectures were uneven from week to week, and the feedback quality varied a lot by assignment, but office hours saved me more than once; I’d say it’s the one lifeline that kept me from total derailment. I barely passed, largely because one memorable week—around the project deadline—felt chaotic and left me scrambling to connect prerequisites to the actual model stuff.

Taking Database Systems this semester has been a surprisingly tough ride, especially since I’m juggling it with two other heavy courses and a midterm-heavy schedule. The workload is very assignment-driven, with deadlines stacking up, but I’ve found Prof. Alvarez’s feedback comes quickly enough to actually adjust between tasks, which helps even when I’m scrambling. I came in worried about the prerequisites, but the material is fairly approachable at an introductory level, though I still learn a lot every week—just not always in the way I expected. The whole thing feels like a mixed bag: I’ve learned tons about schemas and indexing, yet I still dislike how the whole process leaves me drained, like I’m chasing the finish line rather than building something smooth. One moment that sticks is a late-night project where my SQL queries finally streamed together and clicked.

Linear Algebra in the summer term was tough but doable around my full-time job, and the TAs were pretty responsive when I needed quick clarifications. The workload was heavy and deadline-heavy, yet the LMS flow stayed smooth and I mostly kept up. The tooling setup was a pain at first, but once I got used to it, I could focus on the core ideas.

I took Operating Systems with Prof. Alvarez this summer, and the pacing was cramped enough that I felt like I was juggling too many proofs and too little intuition about how things actually run on a machine. The slides were fine as a reference, but nothing stood out as memorable or clearly explained, which didn’t help when I was trying to juggle another hard class at the same time. The group work helped a bit when our team actually communicated, but if one person dropped the ball it dragged the rest of us, so I ended up doing more debugging late in the night than I expected. Tooling setup was a nightmare at the start—getting the environment right felt like fighting through a small obstacle course and it kept eating into actual study time. Quick feedback was a relief because I could course-correct fast, but it didn’t fix the underlying sense that the course itself was useful in theory yet not enjoyable in practice. By the end I felt mixed: I can see the value, even if the daily experience was frustrating, and I’m glad the workload finally coalesced into something I could at least map to a project in my head.

Calculus II was a rough start for me in the program—the first semester, and I was juggling a specialization requirement, plus a midterm crunch that left me sprinting between doors of the library and lecture hall. The material felt like it built on the prerequisites in a sensible way, but the software stack we used was rough at first and only became manageable after a few late-night tweaks and a surprisingly patient peer discussion group that helped more than the official materials. I remember one early moment where I blanked on a substitution during a practice problem and then realized the conceptual thread connected back to the fundamental theorem in a way that finally clicked, which shaped how I approached the rest of the term. The recorded lectures were useful for rewatching, yet they came off as dry, almost lecture-by-lecture narration without much spark, so I leaned on my study group to get the intuition. The pacing felt tight, and I appreciated that the course kind of builds on what you’re supposed to know, but I still disliked the overall experience even as I learned a lot. The best part, honestly, was that the peer discussions often clarified things faster than scrolling through the official handouts.

The Operating Systems course felt like it was built for someone who can blitz through late-night readings, and I’m a returning student who’s rusty, so I kept trying to fit the short evening sessions around the heavy workload. I stayed caught up with nearly every lecture, but the material often felt like it needed a few extra minutes to click—the lectures move fast and the terminology is dense, which left me scrambling to map concepts to the assignments. The tool setup took more effort than I expected for the payoff, especially getting the VM and lab environment ready for the weekly kernels and process scheduling exercises; I remember three evenings just tinkering with the environment before I could run a simple preemption test. Quick feedback helped me adjust, and the TAs were practical and responsive when I asked about why a race condition showed up in a late deadline project, but the overall flow still felt a bit rough and more suitable if you’re in a study group. The biggest annoyance was the exam format for the bonus questions, which seemed to hinge on small edge-cases I hadn’t anticipated, and I wish that had been clarified earlier.

When I took Machine Learning alongside a full-time job, the course started accessible but ramped up fast, and I found myself behind a few times before deadlines finally pulled me back in. The lectures were clear and the pacing reasonable, though the software stack felt rough at first and required some tinkering to get plotting and pipelines moving. I’m comfortable with proofs, but not heavy on systems stuff, so the mid-program core vibe fits: a lot of the theory clicked, and I appreciated how the instructor left room for interpretation on some implementations, which both helped and annoyed me at times. A project around a basic predictor helped me see the ideas in action, even if I wished for a bit more concrete guidance on the data preprocessing steps. Overall, I’m genuinely enthusiastic about where this leaves me.

I just finished Machine Learning with Prof. Cohen in my last semester before graduation, and I barely scraped by after struggling most of the term. The lectures were clear enough when they stuck to the core ideas, but the assessments felt off from what we actually covered in class, which left me chasing a lot of mismatched signals in the weeks leading up to deadlines. Feedback arrived too late to be useful, and when I emailed to ask for quick guidance, the replies were slow right as deadlines hit, which didn’t help my plan at all. The fast scores were nice in the moment, but the explanations behind them were thin, so I never quite understood where I went wrong until I read the TA notes after the fact. I remember one night during a long problem set week where I finally understood how the gradient descent step was supposed to behave after looking at a forum thread the peer TAs shared, which felt like a small win in a sea of confusion. Overall, I learned a lot, but I didn’t enjoy the experience, especially given how the support channels played out and how the course didn’t feel aligned with the lectures.

Calculus II was mostly what I expected, with the lectures feeling solid but not memorable and the slides doing most of the heavy lifting. I went in curious, juggling a full-time job, and I found the course structure worked enough: lots of assignments with deadlines that kept the week honest, and I mostly relied on recordings and my own notes to fit around short evening study blocks. The instructor spoke clearly enough and seemed genuinely invested, which kept me from sinking into frustration when a tricky integration method popped up; still, I wouldn’t call the delivery inspirational, just serviceable. The biggest relief was that the prerequisite gaps I had—especially on improper integrals—got filled better than I expected, which helped me stay on track while balancing work. I liked having a mostly independent workflow, with occasional solo problem sets that matched the pace I could handle, though I did wish there was a bit more explicit guidance for the tougher quizzes. A practical quirk: the grading felt assignment-heavy, and the timing of multiple close deadlines in a single week sometimes pressed at the edges of my evenings, but I managed. Compared to another course from the same term, this one leaned more on consistent practice rather than big exams, and I felt the steady rhythm fit my routine even if the overall energy wasn’t thrilling.

Cyber Security Basics was a lot, but it felt doable because Dr. Singh kept the lectures clean and the pacing was fair, especially given how dense the material gets once you’re deep into threat models. I came in comfortable with proofs but not so much with real sys work, and I found the course’s level nudges from accessible to pretty sharp pretty quickly, which made it feel like the main focus of that term for me. The organization of modules helped me keep track, yet the tool setup was a real slog—configuring the lab environment took more hours than I’d like to admit, and the payoff never quite matched that extra effort. Collaboration expectations were vague, which left my group guessing what counted as a “good” contribution, even though the peer feedback didn’t always line up with the rubric. I learned a ton, especially about attack simulations and the justification of defenses, but I loved the ideas more than the overall experience, and I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared to invest the upfront tool tinkering and you’re ready for a sharp ramp. If you go in with that, it’s worth it.

Taking Linear Algebra with Dr. Chen as my last-semester focus was a mixed bag: the material fit the schedule and finally filled some gaps I worried about, and the LMS flow was smooth enough to keep me sane. The assessments were few but brutal, and the rubric always felt vague, which made grading feel unfairly opaque. Office hours helped a ton when I got stuck on a vectors problem in week eight.

Calculus II in the summer term was rough, but I actually walked away valuing the solid conceptual explanations from Prof. Cohen, even as the thin examples and fuzzy communication about deadlines wore me down while juggling a full-time job. Office hours after a long shift finally clicked one tough topic.

Data Structures kept me curious but kept me honest about where I could keep up. I bought into the topic because I genuinely want to understand how things are organized, and I tried to fit study around short evening sessions, using the lecture notes only when I needed a refresher. Early on I got tangled in the distinction between balanced trees and heaps, which stuck with me and shaped the rest of the term, even though I kept telling myself I’d be better about it next week. The workload felt report-heavy and slow, more time spent parsing a rubric than actually solving a problem, and the timeline for the big weekly submissions meant I used the materials selectively, not consistently. The forums helped some days, but sometimes I felt dismissed when I posted a straightforward question, which didn’t help my motivation, especially when the group work clicked only when everyone was pulling in the same direction. I ended up with a curve-adjusted A, but the real takeaway was a lingering sense that the course fits best if you already know adjacent material.

So here I am in my last semester, coming back to Database Systems feeling rusty, but somehow the course still pushed me to learn more than I expected. The material ramped up in a way that was genuinely challenging, and the weeks with the big project deadlines hit just right—time pressure was mostly manageable, even if I panicked a bit the night before a tricky query optimization task. Dr. Park kept the pace steady, though I kept second-guessing whether the rubric truly captured the effort for the final data-modeling assignment. The software stack started rough for me at first, and the mixed tooling made debugging feel messy, but by midway I could navigate the stack without staring at error logs for hours. One memorable week was the exam with the tricky normalization questions, where I realized I’d forgotten a core concept but recovered with a better approach on the second attempt. Overall, I earned an A after the curve, but the experience left me thinking I learned a lot while not entirely enjoying the ride.

The course dragged a bit in the summer term, but Dr. Singh’s lectures finally clicked once I kept up with almost every lecture and wrestled through the software stack that was rough at first. The pacing felt compressed, and the assessment mix didn’t line up with what we covered in class, but the prerequisites made the material feel like it built on itself. I did end up barely passing after a lot of late nights, and I still remember posting a question in the forum about a tricky packet-filtering example during office hours, which helped more than the slides.

I came back to Cyber Security Basics with genuine curiosity, and while Prof. Cohen is sharp, I felt rusty and the grading rubric was a bit vague, which added a layer of anxiety. TAs are responsive and practical, and the peer discussions helped more than the lectures, especially when it came to the project tool choices. I’ll probably land an A after a curve, but I’m not sure I’d push others to enroll without better clarity on the assessment mix and deadlines. Office hours last month (a quick chat about a randomized checklist I was using) actually stuck with me, though.

I took Operating Systems in my last semester before graduation because I’d heard it would be useful for industry work, and it mostly lived up to that, with the pace feeling a bit heavy for the evenings I could actually block off. Grading felt fairly transparent, though some assignments clearly had room for interpretation and the timing of feedback could arrive too late to help but I could still see where I went wrong, especially on the couple of design questions that depended on a precise wording. The peer discussion sessions helped more than the official materials, which surprised me, and the TAs were consistently responsive and practical when I framed questions around real-world constraints. Deadlines stacked up in a way that caught me off guard, and I ended up juggling short evening study blocks around a few late feedback rounds, which didn’t help the sense of steady progress. I compared it to the prerequisites I survived earlier—the jump felt real but not insurmountable, and I remember one conversation in office hours about synchronization primitives that stuck with me more than the slides. Overall I’d recommend it to others, though you’ll want to plan around the timing and lean on the discussion stuff.

I’m glad I stuck with Operating Systems last semester before graduation, even though the first week left me spinning—my brain did a quick “wait, no, I’m not just proving this, I’m applying it,” and that early confusion still shaped how I approached everything else. Dr. Park is solid, slides are serviceable but not memorable, and the forums helped me feel less alone even when some replies sounded dismissive. The material finally clicked mostly because the proofs-for-soft-intuition stuff felt relevant to my specialization, but the platform quirks and sparse feedback until late in the term kept sneaking in stress I didn’t need. A project and a couple of quotas stuck out, and I remember thinking, “okay, this is how we test an OS scheduler,” even if the road there was rough.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty jumping into the summer OS course while juggling a full-time job, and I still ended up with a mix of frustration and fondness. The setup and tooling to get started were a slog—this isn’t a slick engineering course in practice, and I spent more time fighting the build environment than learning the core ideas, which felt like a poor return on the payoff. The instructor was approachable, and office hours with the TAs were practical and responsive, which helped when I fell behind, but the grading felt opaque and a bit harsher than I expected for a “mid-summer” pace; there were a few quizzes and a couple of bigger projects that mattered more than I anticipated, which amplified the stress. I remember one exam week vividly because of a tricky memory-management question that felt almost like a trap, and I still recall the feedback—very pointed, which I did appreciate even if it stung. Comparing it to another course I took in the same term, this OS class demanded more prior intuition than the ad, and I felt like I walked in with a gap that never fully closed, even when I liked the instructor. Overall, the pain points outweighed the small wins, but I’ll keep the office-hour tips and the TA support in mind if I try again.

I’m in my last semester, juggling this advanced elective on the side of shorter evening study blocks, and the OS course finally clicked after that early confusion about how the scheduler and memory management actually fit together. The lectures were clear and paced fine, but I found myself using the materials selectively—mostly when I hit a tricky topic and then dipping back out for the practical bits, not because I was obsessed with every slide. The TA support was practical and responsive enough when I reached out, which helped when the weekly assignment grading felt inconsistent—some feedback was helpful, other times it felt like a skim. I liked the instructor a lot; the delivery was solid and the examples stayed memorable, but the grading quirks gnawed at me, especially how the rubric seemed to shift between tasks. I tended to work mostly solo, with little peer dependency, and I remember one incident where a late-night code run showed a surprising edge case that forced me to rethink the whole approach to page tables. Overall, the mix felt real: clear instruction, some rough edges in feedback, and a steady grind that fit my schedule.

I took Data Structures mostly to fit my evenings around a tiny schedule, and it feels like I lucked into the right time slot more than I got excited about the subject. Prof. Alvarez is careful and polished, but the help from staff hasn’t quite matched what fellow students figure out in chat groups; we end up helping each other a lot more to keep up. The quick feedback helped me adjust after the midterm, but the report-heavy workload and the tooling glitches dragged deadlines into weeks I didn’t have, which was rough. I remember the moment in week two where I finally understood big-O as a stubborn maze, and that tiny spark carried me through the rest of the term.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty at the start, and this Linear Algebra course kept me on my toes but in a way that wasn’t overwhelming most weeks. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the group work sometimes clicked when the team functioned well, though a few times I felt skating a bit behind the others and relied on the forum to catch up. The workload is heavy with frequent deadlines, and honestly the assignments dominated the rhythm more than I expected; I could race through a problem set and still feel like I’d missed a nuance until the next day. Tooling setup to even begin was more frustrating than it should be—getting the environment ready would eat into study time, which stung since I’m juggling rusty math instincts. Feedback came in patches and often felt sparse until it was kind of late, so I’d finish something and only then see what I did wrong rather than while I was drafting. One concrete moment I’ll remember: I asked about a matrix decomposition in office hours, and the instructor walked through a small but clarifying example on the board that finally clicked, but it wasn’t a common occurrence. Overall, it lined up with my mid-program core expectations, with a solid B that felt like fair alignment with the effort I put in.

I went into the summer term hoping for a smoother ramp-up, but the compressed pace of the Machine Learning course with Dr. Miller felt like sprinting through a dense forest. I juggled it with two other demanding classes, and I found myself cherry-picking the lectures and forum threads when I needed a quick sanity check, especially since the instructions left a lot of wiggle room to interpret things. The forums helped more than they hurt, though a few threads felt dismissive and I had to ignore offhand comments to keep moving. The tool setup was a slog for a while, and the deadlines piled up in a way that caught me off guard, but there was a late-semester turning point when the project finally clicked and I felt genuinely capable, even if the path to get there was messy.

Calculus II with Dr. Park was rough: I used the materials only when I needed them, and the feedback varied a lot by assignment, with administrative instructions leaving too much interpretation. Office hours helped once, but the overall pace left me unsure if the core ideas clicked.

The recorded lectures helped a lot for reviewing tricky definitions, though I’d space out the math-heavy parts because they felt a bit dry in real time. The software stack started rough—several tooling hiccups during the first weeks—yet I managed to push through, and by the midterm I had a better sense of what to optimize in the codebase. I remember Week 6 more vividly for the tricky graph traversal assignment than for the exams, which seemed neutral in fairness but left me unsure about some phrasing on the prompt. Email support was slow right before deadlines, so I relied more on peers and the public forum to figure things out.

I came out with a generally positive take on Linear Algebra, mainly because the exam felt fair and I could gauge where I stood as I studied. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the way Prof. Rios laid out core ideas helped my coding-heavy background map to the theory enough to push through, even though the more abstract parts still slowed me down. TA support was solid and practical when I hit snags, though communications from the admin side could be sloppy, which was a bit frustrating around deadlines. The course is required for my track, and the mix of assessments never quite matched what the lectures emphasized, which was a headscratcher at times, especially since it works best if you already know adjacent material. I learned a lot, but I can’t say I enjoyed the whole ride. One quirky thing I’ll remember: the midterm asked for a small matrix decomposition by hand, which felt oddly at odds with the tool-heavy practice we did in sessions.

Midway through the heavy semester, I’m finding it surprisingly solid to slog through Database Systems even as a newcomer, because the core ideas feel practical rather than abstract. Dr. Park moves the class along at a steady clip, and the few assessments that actually count (the single big data-model assignment and the final design critique) make you tighten your basics rather than drift. I came in hoping it would be useful for industry work, and the hands-on bits with basic SQL topics and a tiny schema design project helped, even if the official materials often feel less helpful than talking things through with peers. The peer discussions matter more to me than the slides or the reading; I end up clarifying tricky points in a way that sticks, which is good when you’re still learning the basics. One memorable week was when we had a surprise design review that forced me to defend a choice in front of the class, which was stressful but memorable and genuinely instructive. The grading rubric feels vague at times, and when deadlines press, email support is slow, but I still feel like the course is teaching me something practically usable.

I enrolled in Data Structures mostly out of genuine curiosity, but I’m left feeling frustrated about how the course organized itself. Dr. Park seems solid, yet the tool setup took more energy than the payoff, and deadlines stacked up in a way that felt catch-up-y more than learning-forward. Most of the work was solo, which didn’t help when motivation was wavering, and the feedback arrives so late I’m already scrambling to fix things for the next deadline. Email support was slow right when we needed quick answers, and I kept thinking this is a required course for the track, so I expected a bit more momentum. Compared to the prerequisite I breezed through, this one slowed me down more than I anticipated.

I took Operating Systems mid-program core, mainly out of genuine curiosity about how things actually run under the hood, and I’ll still say some parts were worth it while others left me frustrated. The course level feels solidly challenging in a good way, and I had to juggle it with two other demanding courses, but I found I could mostly rely on recordings and notes to catch up when I fell behind. The platform quirks were the real stressor for me, though—little quirks in the submission tool and inconsistent timing on auto-graded quizzes made the week feel jittery, not helped by a grading rubric that felt vague and open to interpretation. The exam format and assessment design left me doubting how ideas were being weighed, and the collaboration expectations never felt clear enough to coordinate with my peers without a few awkward back-and-forth messages. Office hours were a rescue, honestly, when I needed a human to sanity-check a kernel-lab question, but it shouldn’t hinge on that. Overall, I’d say the course is more valuable than it’s easy, but I can’t recommend it as-is because the friction in grading and platform design overshadow the good parts.

This term I treated Machine Learning as the main focus while juggling another hard class, and the week-to-week vibe felt uneven; the pacing dragged, and the quick feedback didn’t really explain much beyond a score, even though the assessment felt fair yet exhausting.

Data Structures was fine enough to keep me from losing sleep, even though the organization felt scattershot—recordings and notes kept me afloat during a midsemester sprint, and the TA helped a lot with practical fixes. I liked the instructor, but the grading felt uneven, with frequent deadlines that piled up amid other hard courses; still, the prerequisite gaps got filled better than I expected, and peer discussion helps more than the official materials. I’d only recommend if you’re ready to grind through the chaos.

I took Machine Learning mainly to fit my schedule, not out of pure interest, and juggling full‑time work with limited study time made the workload feel relentless. The assessment mix felt off from the lectures, and even though the TAs were responsive and practical, some feedback came in patches and didn’t always help with the next assignment. I’m glad Dr. Miller knows the theory, but Cyber Security Basics felt more like a sprint than a steady jog, especially in the middle of a brutal semester. The coursework is solid, and I appreciated that it fits best if you’ve seen adjacent material already; I’m comfortable with proofs but not so much with systems work, so I felt a bit behind when we shifted to practical stuff. The course works better with a study group, and I kept thinking a few clearer communications would help, but on a good day the lectures land and the labs are okay. Not sure I’d outright recommend, though I can’t deny it felt useful.

Took Cyber Security Basics while juggling a full-time job, and the lectures from Prof. Rios clicked best on the concepts, though the examples felt thin. The tool setup and the compressed summer pace wore me out, and the project-heavy, high-stakes exams didn’t help my fatigue.

This was my middle-of-a-heavy-semester pick and I kept hoping the schedule would feel lighter, but the Computer Networks intro course still slammed me with back-to-back deadlines and a bunch of platform quirks that stressed me out more than they should. The main thing I remember is feeling like the assessment was fair in scope but exhausting—the quizzes and a midterm stretched out over several days, and even though I earned a solid B, I could feel the effort never quite matching the payoff. By the end I was sort of glad to have something concrete to show for the semester, even if I wasn’t sure I’d choose it again.

Taking Linear Algebra with Dr. Chen while working full-time left me feeling rustier than I expected, and I spent the first couple of weeks chasing my own confusion about vector spaces and bases until I remembered a few key lines from the lecture slides. The lectures themselves were clear and paced well enough that I could keep up when I wasn’t fighting a deadline, but some of the collaboration expectations felt vague, like we were supposed to “coordinate more” without any concrete process, which didn’t help when I was trying to do problem sets after a 10-hour shift. The course surprisingly filled some prerequisite gaps better than I’d hoped—stuff about kernels and images finally clicked after the midterm practice sets—but I still found myself unsure about how the grading would actually treat partial credit on proof-style questions. A small incident with the assignment window slipping a day later on a Friday didn’t derail me, but it did underline that communication around deadlines could be sloppy even if the policies were fine.

I came into Data Structures in my last semester before graduation hoping it would lock in the basics I needed for the specialization, but it mostly felt like an introductory service course in disguise, and I left with more frustration than clarity. The material tied itself to prerequisites pretty cleanly, yet the relevance to what I actually do in my day-to-day projects was thin unless I connected the dots myself, which was hard when the lectures felt skewed toward theory and not the practical bugs I wrestle with at work. The workflow was a pain: tooling setup kept failing, and I spent more time debugging the environment than coding the data structures we were supposed to learn. Assignments piled up with frequent deadlines, and even though the TAs were responsive and offered practical tips, I still felt rushed to produce correct implementations rather than understand why they mattered. I compared it to another course from the same term that leans more on hands-on coding and clearer real-world examples, and this one seemed to miss that bridge, especially when you’re juggling a full-time job. One memorable quirk was a weekly deadline pattern that felt arbitrary, like a reminder to push one small change instead of building a solid understanding, which stuck with me more than any theorem.

I signed up for Cyber Security Basics mainly because I heard it’s useful for industry work, and it fits my plan to study in short evening blocks with recordings and notes. I barely scraped by in Computer Networks, mainly because I had to fit study around short evening sessions and the lectures felt dry on playback, even though the TAs were quick to respond. The Data Structures course felt like a useful hammer when I needed it, even though it wore me out mid-semester. I took Data Structures mainly because it felt like a necessary stepping stone for the specialization, and I was new to the discipline, so I treated it as my main focus that term. Taking Database Systems in the middle of a crazy heavy semester with a full-time job was…messy, but I kept up with nearly every lecture, which I guess helped me not fall behind, even though the pace felt relentless. Dr. Miller is clearly brilliant, but the feedback drips in so late that by the time you’re staring at a graded assignment with a glaring flaw you already know the next deadline is looming again, and you’re scrambling to implement a fix for a problem you didn’t get a heads-up on earlier. The course is very assignment-heavy, with frequent deadlines, and the tooling hiccups didn’t help—deadlines would land during a week when the lab tool would crash or freeze, and you’d be fighting the platform rather than focusing on the concepts. Overall, I’d recommend it broadly, but don’t expect timely, actionable feedback or smooth tooling to carry you through.

I took Database Systems hoping it would be useful for industry work, but I left with more frustration than I expected. Last semester in Linear Algebra, I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the workload felt manageable in a way that matched the effort I put in, even though motivation wavered at times. Calculus II was a mixed bag for me. I’m wrapping up Database Systems in the last semester before graduation, and I used the materials selectively—mostly when I felt stuck rather than for every lecture, which helped a bit with time but left a weird gap in how I connected topics. Kept up with nearly every lecture in Computer Networks with Prof. Rios; the pacing was clear, but the mid‑semester crunch left me frustrated yet fair about the grade, since the assessment felt exhausting despite the quick feedback and mostly individual work.

Linear Algebra in my first semester turned out to be harder in more human ways than I expected. I took Cyber Security Basics while juggling two other demanding courses, so I leaned on the recordings and notes more than live lectures. It’s solid enough if you already know adjacent material, and I learned a lot, but I wouldn’t recommend it overall—the timing and the vibe just didn’t align with my current setup.

The Operating Systems course felt like it was more about surviving the week than building real intuition, especially since I’m returning after a while and felt rusty. Last semester felt like squeezing Linear Algebra into late nights between short evening sessions; the lectures were clear but the grading rubric seemed vague, and I mostly used the materials when I needed them, catching office hours to sanity-check a couple of proofs before the crunch.

There’s a tradeoff here: you get access to practical tools and a rigorous project vibe, but you also juggle a lot of prerequisites, a heavy schedule, and the sense that the tempo shifts from week to week. If you’re balancing this with another hard class, you’ll probably end up prioritizing the parts you can actually use on the next assignment, rather than everything the lectures imply.
