I walked into Computer Networks thinking I’d be fine with the basics, but the course felt heavier than advertised and I kept juggling short evening sessions around work, which made the material feel like it needed more background than it warned about. The lectures were dense, yet I kept up with nearly every one, mostly because the quick questions in office hours with Prof. Alvarez helped me catch the drift even when I didn’t fully grok the underlying model yet. The project-heavy setup and the group work added value only when the team clicked, which happened occasionally and saved me from spinning my wheels on some weeks. I assumed there would be a clearer fit with my prior knowledge, but the prerequisites demanded more crypto and routing intuition than I expected, which left me scrambling for extra readings and a lot of late-night code tweaks. The tool setup felt like a chore for what you actually learned, and I couldn’t shake the sense that the payoff didn’t fully justify the effort. The memory that sticks is staying late in the forum to ask about a flaky packet-trace example, and getting a concrete pointer that helped me finally connect it to the exam-style questions I dreaded. Overall, I learned a lot and still have mixed feelings about the experience.

Overall, Linear Algebra was a rough fit for my mid-program core needs, even though I kept up with nearly every lecture and found the TAs practical. The main letdown was the time-consuming, report-heavy assessments and the dry recorded lectures; I also felt the admin side could be sloppier with communications, though policies themselves were fine. I remember asking a TA about a matrix factorization during office hours and getting a clear, useful pointer, which helped a bit as I juggled short evening study sessions.

Took Machine Learning while working full-time, and I fell behind around deadlines but managed to catch up; Dr. Chen’s lectures were clear, though platform quirks and vague collaboration expectations stressed me out more than the math. Office hours helped once, but the instructions leaving room for interpretation kept gnawing at me.

Summer term of Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez was a mixed ride: solid B, felt it matched the effort, and the LMS flow was smooth, but feedback was sparse until it felt too late—plus the pacing was tight, especially if you’re not already solid on nearby material.

I took Linear Algebra mainly because it’s required for the degree, and I’ve got a pretty solid coding background but weak theory, so I expected to ship through with minimal fuss. The pacing felt off, starting accessible but ramping up sharply before the midterm; by week eight the workload and the abstract stuff collided, and the slides—serviceable but not memorable—didn’t help me stay ahead. Feedback quality varied a lot by assignment, and the tool setup for the platform ate more time than the payoff, which left a sour aftertaste even when a problem finally clicked. I remember failing to make sense of one proof until I dropped into office hours with Dr. Park and we traced a concrete example on the board, which was the one moment where the course felt worth it. I wouldn’t recommend it, but I won’t pretend there wasn’t value there.

I took Cyber Security Basics mainly because it fit my evening schedule, not because I was itching to dive into security topics, and that showed in how I approached the term. The slides were okay—serviceable, not memorable—and I often found myself staring at them late after a long work day, trying to piece together why the concepts mattered. The course felt like a bottleneck: a project-heavy load and a few high-stakes exams that pushed you to hustle, yet the grading quirks and deadlines were easy to miss until the week of crunch time. It’s an introductory service course, so a lot of adjacent material would have helped, but that prereq fit only so well for me, and I struggled more than I’d like because I didn’t have that quick ramp from earlier topics. Collaboration expectations felt unclear, which meant I drifted toward solo work even when group input could have helped my understanding. In the end, I barely passed after surviving most of the term, and while it did push me to manage time better, I can’t honestly recommend it despite some value; comparing it to another course from the term, that one handled pacing and clarity in a much more user-friendly way.

Calculus II was… interesting, I guess. I went into it thinking I’d treat it like the prerequisite, you know, something to get through, but by summer terms I was laser-focused on making it the main thing, since the pacing felt so compressed and I relied a lot on recordings and notes just to keep up. I’m comfortable with proofs, but the week-to-week math felt like a sprint, and the collaboration expectations were never clearly spelled out, which left me guessing who should tackle what in group work. The office hours saved me several times—the instructor would walk through a tricky integration by parts problem and it finally clicked—though the feedback on graded work was always detailed, it took for-ev-er to show up, which was frustrating. The policies themselves seemed fine, but communications around deadlines and policy tweaks were sloppy, which fed into my sense that I was constantly chasing the schedule rather than the ideas. One exam week sticks out: a brutal, long-form setup that felt more punitive than learning, and it’s somehow that memory that keeps looping back. Compared to the easier prerequisite, this felt heavier, and I learned a lot, even if I didn’t enjoy the ride.

Took Database Systems in my first semester, juggling a full-time job, and I genuinely loved the topic enough to push through even when the tooling felt clunky and slow to load. The course built nicely on the prerequisites, and I’d say my solid B matched the effort I could put in between calls and commuting; the feedback came quickly enough to adjust, but the email support when deadlines hit was noticeably slow. The work was mostly individual, and while that didn’t kill collaboration, I appreciated the steady pace and the one project where I dug into a small dataset on my own time, which made me feel like the material stuck. Overall, I’d recommend it broadly.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester and juggling a full-time job, so I mostly notice what actually helps me keep up, not the idealized version of the course. The lectures are clear and the pacing isn’t terrible, but I still feel like I’m chasing the material after hours because my study time is so limited. The peer discussions are the real lifeline here—I rely on them more than the official slides or reading, and I remember one forum thread where a classmate explained a tricky join condition in terms I could actually grok, which stuck longer than the official notes. There aren’t many assessments, but each one matters a lot, and that pressure doesn’t help when I’m trying to squeeze in a project between calls, so I end up overthinking the grading rubric and wondering if my C reflects actual understanding. I like the instructor, and the office hours once I finally attended helped a bit, but they’re not as responsive as the informal student chatter, which feels a bit frustrating. Compared to the prerequisites, this course still feels approachable in some moments yet oddly tougher to translate into confident, steady progress.

Dr. Alvarez’s Machine Learning class hit that sweet spot where the design felt fair but exhausting, and the grading curve kept me honest. The end-of-semester project pushed me to actually connect theory with something tangible, and the built-in tooling worked pretty well once I got through the initial setup snag. Recorded lectures were useful but dry, and while email replies sometimes dragged during deadlines, the course overall filled gaps for me without tipping into chaos.

I’m stuck between liking how the ideas finally clicked when I crunched a few numpy-based linear algebra traces, and hating how the pace during midterms felt like it just kept piling up. Mostly I relied on recordings and notes, since the lectures seemed flaky on follow-up emails, and I kept wishing for clearer guidance from Prof. Alvarez about the project expectations—especially since the report-heavy workload ate into coding time.

I’m a returning student trying to shake off a rusty vibe, and this mid-program core on Database Systems felt like it leaned on interpretation a bit too much in the instructions, even though the LMS and submission flow were smooth as ever. The lecturer is clearly capable and solid with the concepts, but the expectations around collaboration and what counted as “enough” work were oddly unclear, so I spent more time second-guessing than coding. I appreciated the TAs—responsive and practical—especially when I finally dropped by office hours after a stuttered forum question and got pointed, doable guidance. Compared to the easier prerequisite, this one hit harder to translate understanding into the grade, and I’m not sure the C reflects where I actually stand. The pacing and a couple of deadlines feel like they could have aligned better.

I’d say overall I’m torn about the Machine Learning class with Prof. Haddad. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the talks were clear and decently paced, which helped since I’m juggling a full-time job and only have limited weekly study time. But the admin side felt rough—feedback arrives too late to help, and email support drags when deadlines hit, even though the lectures themselves were reassuringly solid. The memorable week was that one midterm Monday where the questions surprised me more than I expected.

I signed up for Cyber Security Basics to meet a specialization, but the exam felt uneven and not very fair, especially with tricky questions around the last module. The forums and office hours helped, though, and I drifted behind then caught up around deadlines.

Calculus II in the summer term felt rushed and a bit disorganized, with Prof. Rios’s lectures piling on equations while the admin guidance left too much to guess. I started engaged but attendance faded; the big pain point was the heavy, report-heavy workload I could never map to the pacing.

Calculus II was this strange mix of "we’re finally tackling the hard stuff" and "why does every assignment feel like a minor apocalypse," and I’m still juggling mixed feelings as I’m wrapping up my last semester before graduation. Prof. Haddad’s conceptual explanations hit the core ideas nicely; when we talked about improper integrals or sequences, I could actually hear the intuition behind the rules rather than just memorize steps. The problem is the examples feel thin, like they expect you to fill in the gaps on your own, and that gap showed up especially on the frequent deadlines—the assignments pile up and the feedback comes in drips, which makes it hard to gauge what’s really expected. Setup for the tools demanded a surprising amount of effort—getting the right plug-ins, navigating the platform, syncing the calculator quirks—and the payoff never felt proportional. I remember one office-hours session where a TA helped me untangle a stubborn convergence issue and explained it with a concrete analogy, which helped a lot, but the email support during midterms was painfully slow. I’m left with mixed thoughts and a sense that the course could’ve used more practice examples tied to the same big ideas.

Data Structures with Dr. Park started off feeling doable and practical, and I appreciated how many of the core ideas connected to real problems I’ve seen in internships, but the summer term pacing was brutal and I felt like we were sprinting through the material. The explanations were solid on the big-picture stuff, yet the examples seemed thin, so I spent more time chasing down tiny edge cases on my own than I expected, especially when the project deadlines loomed. Attendance started engaged, but by mid-semester I found myself dropping in less often, not because I didn’t care but because the compressed pace burned me out and the lecture pace didn’t quite line up with what I needed to internalize the logic. The course leans heavily on projects and high-stakes exams, and honestly I ended up leaning on classmates more than the staff, swapping notes in the forums and grading rubrics, which felt a bit off for a course marketed as guided by a professor. I won’t pretend I loved the ride, but the practical bits—like how the graph traversal patterns translate into real problems—felt worth it, even if the experience itself left me frustrated. I earned a solid B, which matched the effort I put in, given how erratic the support and schedule felt.

I took Operating Systems while juggling two other demanding courses and a full-time job, so my study time was sliced thin and I felt stretched the whole term. The class itself felt useful in theory, but not exactly enjoyable; the lectures bounced around week to week and left me guessing what was actually expected for the next deadline. The project-heavy setup with high-stakes exams didn’t help my already tight schedule, since I barely passed after struggling most of the term and felt behind on most concepts. They quick-graded some scores and then offered thin explanations, so I didn’t get clear feedback on where I went wrong, which left me repeating mistakes in the next assignment. It assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, and I kept wanting a bit more grounding before diving into process scheduling or memory management, especially since I was juggling work and school in parallel. I did have one helpful moment during office hours—one professor gave a concrete example on page replacement that stuck with me, but that was far from the norm. All in all, the course was technically relevant but the delivery and pacing wore me down more than it built me up.

I’m balancing this with another hard class, and the summer pace didn’t help—the week-to-week feel felt uneven and the grading rubric left me guessing what was expected, even after I turned in the report-heavy deliverables. The group work sometimes clicked, other times stalled, and I wish the relevance tied to my full-time job had been clearer; at the end I’d say it helped in places, but I’d probably skip it again given the vibe and the vague rubric. The turning point came late, when a mid-semester setback finally forced a tighter schedule.

I stuck with Computer Networks mainly because I could slot it into short evening sessions, but I left with mixed feelings and a lot of frustration I can’t shake off. The lectures felt well organized, and the exam structure was fair enough, yet I still found the assessment mix off compared to what was actually taught, which didn’t help my weak theory background. I would show up, skim the readings, and only use the materials when I hit a snag, and the email support felt slow right when deadlines got tight. The collaboration expectations were unclear, and the whole admin chatter sometimes came off as sloppy even though the policies aren’t terrible. There were moments the course felt useful, even if I didn’t enjoy it overall, especially juggling it with another hard class.

Machine Learning was the required course for the track I’m in, and honestly I’m glad I stuck with it in the middle of a brutal semester. The assessment design felt solid—projects broke down into manageable pieces and the rubric guided what mattered without punishing late days too harshly, which was a relief for someone new to the discipline. Grading transparency, though, left me with more questions than I’d like: the rubric is vague in spots, so I kept second-guessing whether I was meeting the hidden expectations. The tool setup was a slog—setting up environments and dependencies ate into learning time more than I’d expect, and the payoff didn’t always feel worth it. Still, the course clearly builds on the prerequisites, and I did notice the math clicking a bit more after week six. Help or guidance from staff was spotty; a lot of my peers leaned on each other more than office hours or TAs, which felt both reassuring and a little disappointing. I’ll remember the big midterm around week four—lots of problems that felt like real-lab coding rather than tidy textbook questions, a memory anchor I keep circling back to. Compared to another course I took in the same term, this one felt more useful but less enjoyable, like it’s doing the job even if I didn’t enjoy the grind.

I came away with mixed feelings about Cyber Security Basics, and I wouldn’t say I’d recommend it, even though I did pick up a few concrete things I’ll actually remember. The pace was brutal in the summer term, and the compressed weeks made it feel like we were sprinting from one quiz to the next without fully locking in the theory, which hit someone with my background pretty hard since I can code but I’m weak on the underlying models. Support mostly happened among us peers; I relied on a few classmates who’d swap notes and explain a concept in simpler terms, while the staff felt more like they were distant gatekeepers of the rubric than a resource you could count on. Grading rubrics were vague enough that I spent extra time arguing over a few points, and the feedback varied a lot by assignment—some comments helped for the next task, others were just blunt and late. On the bright side, the accessibility was solid; the online materials were easy to reach, and I didn’t hit any hard barriers to get to what I needed. I did have one moment in office hours where a TA actually walked through a practical example, which helped me see where the theory connects to concrete tasks, even if the overall experience didn’t click for me.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and this intro Database Systems course dragged me back into the weeds more than I expected. Dr. Singh is genuinely enthusiastic, but setup and tool quirks consumed more time than the payoff, and I often felt the prerequisites assume more background than advertised. The late-semester turning point came when a group project finally clicked, showing how the collaboration actually helps when your team pulls together. Overall, I’d not take it again, but it did push me to re-engage just enough.

In Database Systems with Prof. Haddad, I appreciated the clarity of the lectures even as I navigated the heavy mid-semester stretch. I used the materials selectively when needed, and the prereqs built smoothly, though the tooling setup and platform quirks were frustrating at times. I had a concrete office-hours moment where a proof detail clicked, which helped me tolerate the mostly solo work and the stress of administrative friction.

took Cyber Security Basics in the summer term, and the pace felt brutal with deadlines stacking up. Dr. Miller’s slides were okay for keeping up, but the real help came from my peers in quick discussions—the official materials didn’t click as well for me, especially since I’m new to the field. grading felt opaque and when I emailed for a deadline ping, the response was slow, which didn’t help during crunch time.

I took Operating Systems mainly because I heard it would actually help in industry, and it did push me to wrestle with real stuff instead of just memorizing terms. Dr. Singh was pretty clear, and the quick feedback on assignments helped me adjust before the next quiz, which saved me a lot of nail-biting late nights. The platform quirks wore on me, though—some days the grading portal froze or the auto-graded parts felt unfairly harsh unless you hit the exact format they expected. Honestly, this is the kind of course where knowing related material beforehand makes a big difference, and I leaned on office hours to untangle the more stubborn topics; I’ll remember week 6’s memory-intensive process-scheduling assignment as the moment it clicked, even if I wouldn’t sign up for it again.

Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez felt oddly practical on paper but sloggy in reality. I’m comfortable with proofs, but the summer term’s pace and the heavy report load made the later weeks brutal, and the platform quirks added unneeded stress when submitting assignments. I remember one week of the big open-book midterm being a grind, with TAs clarifying questions only in office hours, not forums.

Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez was doable but tiring, and I managed it alongside a full-time job by catching nearly every lecture and relying on my classmates more than official help. The explanations were strong conceptually, but the examples felt thin, so I kept a few notes in the margin and left most problem hints to the study group; there were enough interpretation quirks in the instructions that I felt a bit stuck at times. The midterm pattern and a surprise on the last problem still stick with me.

My biggest gripe was the pacing—the way the term dragged between weeks of dense reading and then a burst of deadlines for projects, it just felt off. Dr. Chen explains things clearly enough on the recordings, but they’re pretty dry, and I found my motivation wobbling despite having decent time to study. Early on I remember getting lost during the initial database design assignment and that confusion hung with me for a while, shaping how I approached later topics. The feedback is thorough when it finally shows up, though the comments arrive late, which doesn’t help when you’re trying to adjust for the next task. I’d only recommend this with a plan to power through and a tolerance for slower progress.

Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Haddad was okay in parts but felt mismatched with my load this last semester before graduation. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, since live lectures moved a bit fast and I had other demanding courses piling up; the pacing was clear enough when I actually watched, but the prerequisite fit wasn’t ideal for me, so I struggled to connect some concepts right away. The few assessments mattered a lot, and the grading comments, while detailed, showed up a bit late, which frustrated my timing for the next tasks. It helps if you have a study group, because talking through the tricky bits actually clicked better than solo notes, and I kept wondering if I’d have benefited from more hands-on practice like a small lab or a concrete project.

Cyber Security Basics with Dr. Miller felt like a solid B overall, given I juggling it alongside a couple of tougher courses. The slides were usable enough to skim when I had a rush week, but nothing in there ever stuck as memorable or sparked real “aha” moments for me. I mostly did the readings and demos on my own time, pulling from the materials only when I needed to cross-check a concept for a quick homework or to prep for a short quiz—time pressure was usually under control, which helped. On grading, the rubric felt vague enough that I worried I didn’t align with exactly what was being looked for, so I tended to aim for practical demonstrations rather than deeper analysis, and that matched my effort with a solid B. The course assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, and that mismatch made the early weeks feel a bit rocky; I found myself leaning on the lectures less and on my own notes more. It was mostly individual work with little peer dependency, so the collaborative angle wasn’t a big factor, and I did end up using the materials selectively when needed, not as a constant reference. Overall, a calm, manageable pace with a couple of rough edges I’ll remember more for the mismatch than for any standout project.

I signed up for Data Structures mainly to fit my schedule, not because I’m wild about theory, and I mostly felt that pressure when it started to ramp up fast. With a strong coding background but shaky theory, I found the early weeks approachable but the later material felt like a wall of details, and the reports dragged on longer than I expected. Office hours with Prof. Cohen saved me more than once—one session where we drilled a recursive solution for a tree problem finally clicked and I walked out thinking maybe I could finish this after all. The course was mostly solo work, which fit my pace, but the time sink of writing and formatting those reports was real, and I barely scratched the surface on the collaboration front.

Taking Computer Networks in my last semester felt like a required rite of passage: I came in hoping it would actually help with industry work, and it did, mostly because Prof. Cohen pushes us to stay on top of quick deadlines and heavy assignments. The tool setup was a slog and the fast feedback helped me adjust, but I still remember fumbling with the lab VM for a good chunk of the term rather than the theory clicking.

Cyber Security Basics was a required starter in the track, and I approached it out of genuine curiosity rather than love for quizzes, but the material cukup kept me kept in. The tooling setup was a pain at first—getting the local dev environment to run for the labs felt like wrestling with a stubborn firewall—and the forums helped only when someone explained things casually, not when you needed a quick fix, which sometimes left me feeling dismissed. The recorded lectures were useful as a backstop, but they were kind of dry, so I only watched them when I hit a concrete snag like the week we did the network scanning assignment, where the timing and hints in the video mattered more than the slide bullets. I learned a lot from the concrete office-hours chat I had about a tricky packet-filtering rule, which helped me see where my understanding was thin, even if the feedback on later submissions varied in usefulness. I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared to deal with setup friction and don’t expect a lot of warmth from the forums; I finished unsure if the grade truly reflected what I understood, but I did feel the topic clicked in the end.

I’m a returning student who felt a bit rusty, and Data Structures drove that home in small, nagging ways. The early confusion I had about Big-O notations and how the hash table behaved in practice stuck with me, shaping how I approached later chapters even though the lectures themselves got pretty dry once we hit the code. I started off actually engaged, but my attendance faded mid-semester as the weekly rhythm got hard to keep up, and the few big assessments mattered a lot, so the deadline pressure kept pulling me back in. The software stack was rough at first—setting up the environment felt like wrestling with a stubborn toolchain—but by midterms it was manageable enough to push through, especially with TAs who were responsive and practical in their fixes. Recorded lectures helped some, though I wished they carried a bit more energy; they’re useful when I’m rereading code, not so much in live concentration. A single project—building a small graph library—felt meaningful, with a clear result that helped me gauge what I actually understood, even if the grade didn’t fully reflect my grasp.

When I took Operating Systems with Prof. Haddad, I was juggling a full-time job, so I came in with decent practical patience but less stamina for the lengthy late-semester deep dives. The class felt like an introductory service course that’s heavy on concepts you should know before you start, and I found that the quick feedback from TAs was a lifeline—practical, punctual, and often focused on what would actually help code faster rather than grand theoretical wins. The grading rubrics, though, felt vague, so I was left guessing what counted as “clear understanding,” which was frustrating when the deadlines piled up and the project grew more intricate than I expected. I remember a turning point around week 11, when a late-night debugging session finally clicked about process scheduling, and I realized I’m not actually terrible at this—just needed a bit more structured practice than the course promised. The prerequisite feel mattered; it works best if you’ve already touched some of the adjacent material, otherwise the gaps show in practical questions. Still, the fast arrival of scores without thick explanations left me wanting more context, and I probably wouldn’t take it again, even though the knowledge did stick in a few stubborn moments.

Starting my first semester in the program, I focused on Computer Networks with Dr. Miller and found it mostly calm, but the hit-or-miss collaboration expectations left me puzzled more than once. The course does build on the prereqs, but I remember an early moment when I misread a deadline and spent a night frantically patching a network diagram for the next day’s handout—that confusion set the tone for the term. Office hours saved me more than once, even when the questions were simple but persistent, and the report-heavy workload felt exhausting despite being “fair” in grading. Time pressure was manageable most weeks, and I did end up making it the main focus, though I still wonder if the collaboration structure could be clearer.

Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad felt useful for getting basics straight, but the platform quirks and the vague grading rubric made it stressful to keep up. TAs were responsive, though the report-heavy deadlines piled up and the process wasn’t enjoyable.

First, Dr. Chen’s lectures gave big-picture ideas, but the examples were thin and hard to map to real code, and the email support during deadlines was slow; I faded from attendance midterm though I juggle other tough courses.

Taking Operating Systems in my first semester, I appreciated how the course pacing moved fast but kept me pushing at the right moments, and the organization helped me chart deadlines even when tooling glitches stretched a week of crunch time. The exams felt fair in structure but exhausting because the workload piled up, and Prof. Haddad’s office hours finally clicked once I hit a snag on a memory-management quiz. The forums helped, though sometimes responses felt a bit curt; still, the prerequisite gaps got filled better than I expected, and I’d still recommend it to others entering the track.

I signed up for Data Structures mainly to fit the schedule around my full-time job, and I kept up with nearly every lecture, but I was never sure the pacing would actually match how little time I can carve out each week. The instructor explains concepts well, though the real-world examples felt thin, which made the harder parts drag on longer for me given my limited study hours. TAs were responsive and practical when I reached out, which helped a lot on debugging a stubborn linked-list exercise, but the platform quirks—skipping a submission window or losing a draft—added avoidable stress, so I dreaded the weeks when the grading system hiccuped. I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and the feedback Quality bounced around depending on the assignment, which left me guessing how to improve for the next one. It’s not all bad; I compared it to an easier prerequisite and felt the jump was bigger than I anticipated, yet I kept thinking I could have managed better if the examples had clicked earlier. By the end I was conflicted enough to change my mind mid-review, and I suppose that wandering sense is the core takeaway I’ll remember.

This course felt like a gentle dunk into a big pool: lots of concepts spread out in a way that makes sense once you’ve got the basics, but I’m still figuring out how it all fits together. The explanations are strong on the ideas, but the concrete examples sometimes feel thin, so I left a lot of sessions with a vague sense of “okay, I sort of get this, now what do I do with it?” My biggest frustration came from the instructions: they often felt open to interpretation, and I’d end up guessing what the TAs actually wanted on the weekly assignments. On the plus side, the TAs are responsive and practical; I could email a question and get a concrete debugging path or a quick demo in the chat, which helped when I was trying to fit study around short evening sessions. The course builds on the prerequisites and the project, a straightforward coding task with a simple dataset, helped me see where the math shows up in practice, even if I’m still unsure about the best way to illustrate the ideas. By late October, I realized I’ve been leaning more on recordings and notes than live lectures, which felt like the turning point: I finally started tying the theory to a tiny, real model I could explain to myself. Overall, it’s a decent intro, just not as tidy as the easier prerequisite I’m used to.

Calculus II ended up feeling like a last-minute scramble that I mostly pushed through by watching recordings and scribbling notes, since I was juggling a tighter schedule than I’d hoped. I came out feeling the course filled gaps in the prerequisite stuff better than I expected, but the grading was a constant thorn—the project heavy weight plus high-stakes exams left me stressed and hashtag barely passed after I struggled most of the term. I’m a returning student who felt rusty, taking Database Systems mainly out of genuine curiosity, and I can tell you the pacing hit me mid-semester like a wall of heavy reading and deadlines. Office hours became my lifeline—one TA walked me through a tricky normalization problem and saved me from bombing a quiz, which was the small bright spot in a lot of tooling hiccups that stretched deadline weeks. I didn’t expect to walk away with a tidy conclusion, but I’d still rank the effort as a solid B that matched the energy I put in, even if I wouldn’t take the course again.

So I’d say Calculus II was… fine, at the middle of a heavy semester I just barely got through it. The lectures feel useful when I’m watching the recordings, but they’re pretty dry and I still feel rusty as a returning student in the middle of a heavy semester. Cyber Security Basics became my main focus this term, and I stalled after the first few weeks with a failed grade, even though the content wasn’t all bad. The lectures are dry but the study group helped, and I remember week five’s simulated breach assignment more than anything.

Starting OS with Prof. Haddad felt like wading into the basics while everyone around me already knows a few adjacent topics, which didn’t help my confusion early on. The TA support is practical and responsive, but the fast feedback with only a thin explanation leaves me guessing how to fix things; the assignment-heavy pace under mid-semester fatigue doesn’t help. I recall my first week— scrambling over a simple process scheduling bug— and that moment shaped the rest of the term more than any lecture.

I picked Cyber Security Basics because it fit my late-evening study slots, and I’ll admit the lecturer kept the momentum even when my brain was half-asleep after a long coding session. The exams felt fair enough once I got into the groove, and the lecturer’s explanations helped me connect the dots from the prerequisites to the mid-program core stuff, even though my strength is hands-on code and not theory. I’m glad I stuck with it, even though I’d probably skip it again if I could redo my schedule, because it did push me to adjust my study rhythm, not to mention the time-consuming reporting workload that dragged me into moments of frustration.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty coming into Machine Learning with Dr. Park in the middle of a heavy semester, and the experience left me a bit torn. The forums helped when people chimed in, though some responses felt dismissive, like we were overthinking it, not solving the core issue I had. Attendance pattern aside, the project felt doable in principle, but the week-to-week cadence and the flaky tooling turned it into a slog. I did learn a lot in the end, even if the ride was rough: I’d still recommend it to others who can tolerate the hiccups, though I’d warn about the mid-semester crunch and the sometimes unhelpful admin friction.

Summer term was a compressed slog; the advanced Linear Algebra toolbox felt usable, and the quick feedback helped tweak proofs, but setup was a hassle and the lectures were dry. TAs were practical, though, and I compared it unfavorably to the easier prerequisite.

I took Computer Networks as my main focus this term, since it was a required track course and I was counting on it to pull my GPA up before graduation, but I’m still unsure whether I actually understood what we covered. The lectures, while all recorded and handy to replay, felt dry and hard to stay awake through, and the software stack we started with was rough at first but ended up manageable after a lot of fiddling. The instructor I liked enough—clear explanations in class—yet I couldn't shake the sense that the grading moved in ways that didn’t help much with actual understanding, especially since feedback landed too late to fix things before deadlines piled up. The deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and the email support when I hit a deadline was slower than I’d hoped, so I sort of did most of the midterm scrambling on my own. I compared it to another course from the same term, which had sharper timing on feedback, and that lingering contrast didn’t help. Overall, I’m torn: I’m glad I stuck with it for the relevance, but I’m not sure the clarity or timing quite matched my expectations.

Taking Database Systems as my first real dive into the discipline, I was hooked early on by the idea of what a database actually does for a project, even though the software stack started out rough for me. I appreciated that Prof. Rios kept the lectures approachable, but the big gap came with feedback—grading comments were detailed yet delayed, which made it hard to learn from early mistakes in time for the next assignment. In the end, I relied a lot on peers for help since staff reach felt sporadic, and the first couple of weeks with the tooling were rough but I learned to push through. Some days I stayed curious, others I just showed up and tried to keep pace.

Taking Computer Networks with Prof. Haddad was doable since I kept up with nearly every lecture; the workload felt doable and group study helps, but the tooling setup and variable feedback timing annoyed me a bit—office hours helped after a rough assignment.

I took Calculus II in the summer term mainly to fit my schedule, not because I’m dying to dive deeper into limits, but I did end up liking Dr. Miller’s lectures for their clarity and steady pace. The mid-semester crunch hit me hard, and the grading felt inconsistent—like the same problem could earn different points depending on which TA graded it, which was frustrating given my relatively weak theory background. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, and the TAs were practical and quick to respond, which helped when I needed quick handoffs during a code-heavy week. One memorable week was the monster exam in week 6 that felt more like a speed-test than a calculus check, and I’ll admit I missed a few subtle steps I’d hoped to catch in time. I’d only recommend the course if you’re prepared to put in the extra prep work.

The course felt like the main thing I had to push through this term, since the OS material was a required piece of my degree and I came back rusty after a few years out of school. A late-semester turning point stood out for me: a practical project tying process scheduling to a real workload pattern, which kept the larger picture in view despite the rough patches.

Cyber Security Basics was a slog I stuck through while juggling a full-time job, and I came out with mixed feelings. The lectures were clear and paced well enough for the most part, which helped since I was juggling late client calls and coffee-fueled coding sessions, but I still felt like the theory side didn’t land for me—my strong coding background saved me in some hands-on parts, yet the abstract concepts didn’t click as smoothly as I’d hoped. The course is clearly a required piece of the track, and the project-heavy approach with high-stakes exams meant the score pattern came fast and furious, even though feedback explanations felt thin and hurried after each deadline. Setup for the tools took more effort than the payoff deserved, honestly; I remember fighting the environment before I could even run a basic lab, which left a sour taste early on and colored the rest of the term. A rough mid-semester crunch didn’t help, and I still recall an early confusion about threat modeling that shaped how I approached everything after, like a stubborn breadcrumb. Overall, I’d say there’s organization and some useful structure, but the mismatch between prerequisites and my background left me with a lingering sense that I could have learned more with different pacing.

Machine Learning with Prof. Rios was my main focus this term, and I barely passed after wading through the term while juggling another hard class. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, and the course felt like it helps more if you already know adjacent material; I struggled until the end with the prerequisites. Group work helped when the team clicked, but feedback was sparse and came too late for my midterm prep. I’d only recommend it if you come in prepared.

Taking OS with Dr. Miller felt like a required hurdle I trudged through while juggling a full-time job, and it left me with mixed, stubborn impressions. Operating Systems with Dr. Singh started accessible but ramps up fast, and I relied mostly on recordings and notes; the biggest drag was the tool setup and the heavy, project-heavy workload, with deadlines piling up and some instructions leaving too much room to interpret.

The Machine Learning course in my last semester before graduating had its moments, but I walked away with more patience for the next grading curve than genuine awe. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I spent more time decoding the platform quirks than appreciating the ideas, which didn’t help since I come from a strong coding background and weak theory—yet somehow it still filled in a few prerequisite gaps better than I expected. Data Structures in the summer term felt rushed and a bit rough at the start, with the software stack proving rough for a while before it finally settled into something manageable. Professor Haddad explains concepts well, yet the examples tend to be thin and I used the materials only when I needed them, especially after the turning point in week six when I finally grokked how to tie the proofs to the data structures in a project I barely finished.

Calculus II this summer felt like sprinting through a maze with a couple of really solid maps at the start and then a lot of dead ends. The platform often hiccuped right before a submission window, which made a few deadlines feel like they stretched out into days rather than hours, and the staff answering questions felt slower than the students just helping each other out. Overall, I’d still recommend it, but it’s not the most enjoyable ride; it’s useful, even if the delivery sometimes felt thinner than the ideas.

Data Structures with Dr. Singh was a first-semester scramble: the prerequisites felt heavier than advertised, yet the work around group projects added value only when the team actually functioned. The LMS was smooth and deadlines came with fast feedback, though the explanations were sometimes thin. I managed it alongside full-time work and a couple of other demanding courses, and I’d still say the course is doable if the group clicks.

I’m new to ML, so I came into the introductory service course this summer with the goal of learning the basics fast, and I ended up making it my main focus for the term because the pace felt manageable most weeks and the deadlines kept me on track. The course was fine to get through, but the pacing in the summer term felt compressed and it kicked up a lot of time-pressure. I fell behind, caught up near deadlines, and the report-heavy workload plus rough tooling setup made the whole thing feel rough at first.

Calculus II with Dr. Miller during the summer term felt rushed and a bit scattered, especially as attendance dropped after the first few weeks; quick feedback on exams came just fast enough to juggle the next problem set, and I relied on classmates more than the instructor for quick clarifications, like the week-6 project constraints.

The lectures were clear and paced fine, but the exams felt exhausting and sometimes unfair for my understanding, especially balancing it with two other tough courses. I enjoyed Prof. Cohen’s passion, but the grading felt slow and opaque, which left me frustrated as a full-time student with limited study hours. The course helped with practical ideas, and the LMS flow was smooth, though some tooling felt clunky and the mid-term crunch was brutal.

I jumped into Cyber Security Basics thinking it’d be a stepping stone, but it became my main focus that term, handled alongside another tough class. took the Machine Learning course this summer while juggling a full-time job, and it was rough in pacing and tools. the lectures felt a bit rushed and the code-heavy labs with the new framework were hard to keep up with, even with office hours that saved me once or twice a week; i still ended up relying on the forums for quick clarifications between deadlines. i’m not sure i’d recommend it for someone needing steady, predictable momentum, but the quick feedback loop did help me adjust as i went.

Calculus II was a mixed ride for me, juggling a full-time job and limited study time, and I fell behind with the weekly pace but managed to catch up around deadlines. took database systems with a full-time job last semester, and Alvarez’s grading comments were detailed but arrived late, which made it hard to plan. i remember the early confusion about joins shaping the rest of the term, and the office hours were a lifesaver when i could actually get in.

I’m in the Linear Algebra required track, and I’d say Dr. Miller is great in the sense that I came away liking the instructor, but the grading felt piling on and a bit disjoint from what we covered. Calculus II with Prof. Rios in the summer term was one of those courses where the pace felt compressed, but I needed it for the specialization, so I stuck with it anyway. Still, I managed to land an A after a curve, which was enough to keep me moving, and I learned a lot, even if I didn’t love the experience. It helps a lot if you’ve got a study group, since the material rewards discussion more than solitary brushing up. Overall, I barely passed, but I remember enough specifics to feel it was real.

Memo to self: Calculus II felt like I was re-learning how to think in math, but the gaps didn’t crush me since I had time, even if motivation wandered. I started the summer term hoping Cyber Security Basics would be practical for industry work, and it did fill some prerequisite gaps, especially after the first week. The tool setup was a slog, butOffice Hours saved me once I got a concrete answer about the lab assignment.

It helps if you have a study group, because I definitely relied on others to decode the assignments like the week-4 lab report and the incident-response quiz.

I kept up with nearly every lecture for Cyber Security Basics, and I appreciated how quickly Prof. Alvarez replied with notes that helped me adjust my approach after a busy week at work. The course felt a bit uneven week to week, though, and a lot of the work ended up being report-heavy and time-consuming, which didn’t fit well with my short evening blocks. I liked the instructor, but the grading sometimes felt unclear, almost like I was weighing the same effort against different expectations each week. The small project on mapping a basic threat model helped me see practical stuff, even if I struggled to fit the long writeups around my full-time job. Overall, I’m unsure whether I’d recommend it.

Looking back, I’m still torn about Machine Learning in my last semester before graduation. The lectures were clear and paced fine, which helped since I’m new to the discipline and trying to learn the basics around short evening sessions, but the way the course ties everything to a big project and high-stakes exams felt overwhelming after a rough mid-semester crunch. The grading rubric, though, seemed vague to me—like there were hidden expectations I didn’t catch until a late feedback email, which left me second-guessing how to allocate my effort. Most of my work was solo, with little peer dependency, so I found myself guessing at the standards more than getting guidance from others. The project component mattered a lot, and I appreciated some hands-on tool work, though it also emphasized a performance-orientation that clashed with my slower progress. I’d still recommend it broadly, since the fundamentals finally clicked in some weeks, but I’d warn a new student that the evaluation vibe and the midterm squeeze can make the experience feel rough and uneven. Overall, it’s a mixed bag that I’m glad I stuck through, even if I’m not confident I’d repeat it exactly.

I signed up for the Machine Learning course mostly to fit the schedule this semester, and it felt right to push through a heavy midterm stretch, even though I was juggling a ton of other readings. I appreciated the instructor’s explanations when they happened, but the grading didn’t land the same way for me; I liked the vibe in lectures, but the feedback came too late or felt sparse, which is rough when you’re trying to catch up around deadlines stacked up unexpectedly. Group work added value when the team actually pulled together, though my own attendance slipped as the semester dragged on and I fell behind before sprinting to catch up at the last minute. The heavy report requirements were the real time sink, and it’s hard to separate the workload from the practical application you can actually take away, but I did learn a few solid tactics for feature selection that stuck with me.

Data Structures felt like a tough climb while juggling a full-time job, with uneven weeks and tooling hassles that blew deadlines; I barely passed, but the prereqs finally clicked, and I’d still wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push my limits.

The summer term compressed pacing made it hard to stay with the lectures, and the software stack started rough but got manageable later; I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and the group work helped only when our team clicked, not always. I needed Computer Networks for a specialization, and Professor Haddad generally delivered clear lectures with decent pacing, plus the LMS and submission flow were smooth, which kept me from spiraling during busy weeks. I started out engaged and kept up fairly well, but my attendance faded mid-semester as the workload piled up and the week-before deadlines turned into time-pressure that felt manageable most weeks yet still exhausting. The course leaned heavily on reports, which felt time-consuming and sometimes dragged out more than I wanted, even though I learned a lot from the material and the practical examples we discussed in class. I came away with real insight into how networks scale, though there was this ongoing sense that the collaboration expectations were unclear, and I wasn’t sure who was supposed to do what in group tasks. A small but memorable hiccup: a deadline pattern around midterms that didn’t align with my other courses, which made one project feel more stressful than it should have. Overall, I’d recommend the course broadly, even as I worry I’d have preferred a bit more structure around teamwork and some lighter assessment pacing.

Calculus II was useful for industry work, and the lecturer made the tricky parts feel doable with steady explanations and a calm pace, which helped since I’m juggling a full-time job and don’t have much weekly study time. The big downside for me was the exam fairness—some questions felt like traps that hinged on things I didn’t quite catch from the lectures, while the grading didn’t always reflect the effort I put in during the week. I appreciated that the course builds on the prerequisites, and the lecturer clearly connects the ideas, but it didn’t help my situation when feedback arrived too late to fix a missed concept before the next test. Email support tends to be slow right around deadlines, which was frustrating, and the structure mostly encouraged solo work with little peer dependency, so I felt a bit isolated grinding through the practice problems. I’ll admit I was motivated by a belief it would be useful in industry, and the office hours—where I asked about a stubborn integration method—felt like a solid anchor in a stressful week. The time pressure was generally manageable, but the constant pace and the mixed signals on grading left me with mixed feelings.

Honestly, I’m mid‑semester exhausted and frustrated enough to say this course could have fit better with how I actually study, given I’m juggling a full‑time job and only carve out time here and there. The structure feels messy and the calendar seems to bend around admin quirks more than actual learning, with policies fine in theory but communication slipping so I’m left guessing what’s due or where the file lives. I used the materials selectively—when I needed a quick reference during a late-night coding sprint—but the tools grind, deadlines pile up, and weeks of pressure tend to spike right after a vague feedback ping that arrives when I’m already past the appointed window. We had a couple of real assess­ments that actually mattered, and for once I felt the weight of “this one counts” in a way that made me cut corners elsewhere, which is ironic. A turning point came when a late‑semester assignment exposed how sparse feedback can be, and I realized I’d missed an important nuance in the OS scheduling section because I didn’t know where the instructor would weigh it in, not because I didn’t understand the concept. Calculus II was a required stop for me since I’m trying to stay practical for industry work, and I juggled it alongside a couple of other tough classes, so I used the materials selectively rather than devouring everything. The lectures felt dry, but the recordings were usable in a pinch when I needed to refresh a concept before finals, and I actually appreciated that the office hours were a real rescue when I got stuck on a tricky substitution problem. My big gripe is the exam setup: the grading felt uneven and sometimes seemed to hinge on quirks that weren’t clearly communicated, which left me frustrated even though I could follow the logic in class. I liked the instructor a lot—clear explanations, some relatable anecdotes—but I wasn’t fond of how the policy communications came across; it felt sloppy and left me guessing about deadlines one week to the next. Overall, the course gave me a practical toolkit, but the inconsistent exam and murky policies stuck with me more than I’d hoped.

I left the machine learning intro with a mix of relief and fatigue, sure I learned enough basics to feel capable but not energized to go deeper. The workload felt doable and practical enough to slog through, yet the weekly rhythm was rough—some weeks the pace was uneven and the grading seemed inconsistent. The software stack started rough but became usable, and I appreciated that it built on solid prerequisites, even if I wished the motivation kept more consistent.

Took Computer Networks last semester while working full-time, and I barely kept up with almost every lecture; the concepts clicked, but the examples felt thin. The group study thing helped, and the midterm week’s tricky routing question still sticks in my memory.

This course was a slog my last semester, and I’d only push it with serious prep. Calculus II felt like the last big push before graduation, and I was juggling it alongside a couple of other heavy courses, so the workload landed as a steady mountain rather than a cliff—manageable enough to keep momentum, but with enough deadlines and a midterm crunch to keep me honest. A small, memorable note: the course managed to feel skippable after the easier prerequisite, but then the problems still showed up demanding solid work, which left me glad I hadn’t treated it as optional.

Minding the heavy mid-semester grind, I stuck with Machine Learning mostly because Prof. Cohen is solid when you actually grapple with proofs, even if the systems side felt rough at first. The workload sits about neutral, but the assessment—the long report stack—felt exhausting and time-consuming, especially since I was juggling another hard class; the curve helps, but it never fully takes the edge off. Support from peers was more reliable than staff, and the software stack started stubborn, with quirks in the tooling that were annoying before I found workarounds. A few communication missteps from admin left a nagging sense that policies were fine on paper but sloppy in practice, yet the core lectures kept me engaged enough to push through.

Calculus II was a mixed ride for me this summer. I took it mainly because I needed it for a specialization, and the pacing felt compressed, which didn’t help my motivation much. I stuck with OS in this weird evening slot, trying to squeeze around short sessions and still keep up, and I’ve got mixed feelings. Fell behind early, but I caught up around deadlines, mostly because peer discuss-ions helped more than the slides. Dr. Chen’s concepts click, but the examples were thin and the platform quirks stressed me out during practice attempts.

I’d say the course was okay to start, but the setup dragged more than I expected once summer term hit its compressed pace, especially since I’m juggling a full-time job and only get a few solid evenings per week. I took Cyber Security Basics while juggling a full-time job, and I’m still hashing out how I feel about it. Database Systems under Dr. Miller has felt like a solid backbone this semester, especially since it’s a required course for the track and the prerequisites thread together nicely with where I’m headed. I kept up with nearly every lecture in Linear Algebra, and the course overall felt like a solid advanced elective that built nicely on the prerequisites, especially for someone juggling a full-time job. I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and this advanced Linear Algebra course with Dr. Chen hit me with practical payoff even if the setup was clunky. The tooling setup took more effort than I expected, which sunk some part of the learning payoff because I kept wrestling with config issues before I could actually start the problem sets. Deadlines came in fast, and the assignments were heavy on practice, which actually helped me salvage some intuition I’d lost, but the communication around policies felt sloppy at times—nothing dramatic, just little mixups that made admin feel less smooth. I compared this term to another course in the same term and found that one offered clearer project scaffolding, whereas this one pushed me to rely on notes and substitute explanations to fill gaps. I’d recommend it only with real preparation and a plan to grind through the early weeks; otherwise it’s easy to fall behind, but I did learn a lot if you stay on top of the recordings and the frequent problem sets.

This summer term moved fast, and I had enough time but motivation kept drifting, so I mainly stuck to solo work and a few late-night study sessions. Prof. Rios’s lectures were clear and the pacing decent, with the project on indexing that actually helped me see how the pieces fit, but the admin stuff left room for interpretation and the support mostly came from us students helping each other.

I took Linear Algebra mainly to fit my schedule this semester, not because I’m obsessed with vector spaces, and that bias colored my whole experience. The course works better if you have a study group, since the in-class work often isn’t enough to untangle the proofs or the little algebra tricks that suddenly show up on the quizzes. I failed and still have mixed feelings: I didn’t see the point of some of the more abstract sessions, yet a later turning point clicked enough to keep parts of the theory in mind for the next course. The feedback comes sparse until it’s basically overdue, which makes it hard to course-correct, especially when the grading quirks—like a late-week assignment pattern and a single heavy take-home exam—feel unpredictable. The whole thing assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, and I wish the materials were clearer about what you’re supposed to have nailed down before you start, but some days the actual problem sets do push you to think in a way you don’t expect.

I took Operating Systems with Dr. Miller mostly because it was required for the degree, and as a returning student I felt rusty enough to stumble through the early weeks. The course leaned heavy on assignments with tight, frequent deadlines, and the grading rubric always felt vague to me, like I wasn’t sure what exactly would swing a grade until it did, which added a quiet anxiety. I remember one early moment—an API mismatch that about made me abandon a project—that shaped how I approached the rest of the term, and I recall feeling uncertain about whether my late-night fixes actually aligned with expectations. Calculus II with Dr. Miller was tough but builds on the prereqs, and I barely passed after a midterm crunch; the weekly homework felt heavy and the platform quirks added unnecessary stress, though group work helped when our team clicked. Memory: that week with the integration by parts quizzes.

Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Cohen was tough to juggle alongside two other demanding courses, and I found the instructions left too much room for interpretation; the project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams didn't help, even though the lectures were clear and pacing reasonable. Calculus II felt like the required checkpoint I had to clear, and I tried to fit it around long evening shifts. The assessment mix didn’t line up with what the lectures emphasized, and I’d sometimes feel exhausted by the pace even though the work was fair.

Calculus II became the main focus of my term, and I came in with a strong coding background but basically no deep theory, so I expected to hack through but ended up wrestling with the abstractions anyway. I’d say the course was worth it for the core ideas, but I’m not sure the grade line reflected what I actually understood. The best part by far was the office hours; when I finally sat down with someone who could walk through the reasoning for a tricky pointer or a stack problem, the course suddenly clicked enough to keep plugging away. I struggled more than the advertised prerequisites suggested, and it sometimes felt like we needed a stronger foundation before jumping into the more abstract data structures, which made the grading feel harsher than I expected. The software stack started rough for me at first but loosened up as I kept tweaking the setup, which helped a bit in the end, especially when I compared it to another course from the same term that felt smoother overall. The late-semester turning point came when I realized I could salvage some momentum, but the overall vibe remains torn—a relief to have finished, with a lingering sense of what still feels beyond reach.

I found working with a study group mattered a lot; we split labs and it kept the material from flying by too quickly. My grade hovered around the C range, and I’m not sure that reflected my understanding, given the one tricky project and the exam format that relied on quick recall under time pressure. One concrete pain point: the deadline pattern felt uneven, with a tough lab due right after a midterm, which was rough while also taking another hard class. Overall, it helped more than it hurt, but I wouldn’t take it again if I could avoid it.

I did appreciate a late-semester turning point where I finally tied the project to the exam format, but the feedback came sparse until it felt too late to adjust. If you’re going in, be prepared to lean on the late push and maybe have a backup plan for keeping up, and you’ll probably get something practical out of it. I’d recommend it only if you’re ready to invest extra effort up front.
