I took Operating Systems because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and I’ll admit the workload was manageable enough to keep me motivated, even if the weeks felt chaotic with deadlines stacking up. Prof. Alvarez’s lectures felt uneven week to week, and the grading rubric was vague, which didn’t help when I was already scrambling to fit short evening study sessions around everything else. Office hours were a rescue—one late session saved my grade when I was barely passing after a rough stretch. Group work added value only when the team actually functioned, otherwise it felt like a drag, and I kept thinking I should have pushed the project to be more solo. Still, the course taught me practical stuff I’ll actually use, so I changed my mind midterm on how to approach the OS questions.

The Database Systems course started approachable enough, but the ramp-up hit hard and left me scrambling despite a solid coding background. I used the materials selectively—mostly when a project deadline loomed—yet I still found the lectures and readings scattered and hard to map to real tasks. One early confusion about normalization stuck with me and kept shaping how I approached later topics, which didn’t help when the grading felt like it arrived late and sometimes harsh. The forums helped, but conversations could feel dismissive, and the platform quirks added needless stress during quick deadlines. I’d probably recommend it only if you’re prepared to push through a rough start and tolerate some friction.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Linear Algebra, but the lectures felt rushed and the lecturer often drifted off into side comments I didn’t find helpful. The fast-clip online platform quirks plus thin explanations for the quick-grade quizzes fed my stress, especially since I’m juggling a full-time job. Peer discussion saved me more than the official materials, and the project on eigenvectors felt useful, even if the grading quirk at 60% of the final came out of nowhere.

Looking back, this first semester in Machine Learning felt like trying to keep up with one good lecture per week while juggling two other demanding courses. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, since live interactions weren’t the strong suit and the staff answered questions slowly; my progress was hampered by the assumption that we already knew more math than I actually did. The assignments varied a lot in how helpful the feedback was, and the mix of what we were tested on didn’t always line up with what we covered in lectures. Still, I walked away with a decent handle on proofs and a few concrete skills, like debugging a small numpy project on my own terms, even if the overall pace exhausted me.

The class was a slog but kept me honest: the workload piled up fast, and the project-heavy exams kept me scrambling, yet the peer discussions saved me more than the official lectures, especially when deadlines stacked up and I just needed one practical hint.

I took Database Systems in my last semester, and I’ll admit I left with mixed feelings. The lectures were clear and the pacing was reasonable, but the material felt oddly opaque at times, especially when we dove into indexing and query plans—the explanations skimmed over some transitions and I ended up chasing gaps on my own. The course mostly kept me on my own; collaboration was minimal, which didn’t help when I hit a puzzling week with the big project and a midterm back-to-back. The weekly assignments were concrete, like sorting through a small schema and writing a few proofs, but feedback came fast yet felt thin, missing the rationale behind some grading quirks. One memorable week was the practical exam where we had to tune a query on a live dataset, and I appreciated that some gaps in prerequisites got filled, even if I still had to puzzle through the last part on my own.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and Cyber Security Basics barely kept me from sinking into a fog of rusty assumptions. The first week there was a moment I misread an attack scenario in the forum thread and spent days chasing a red herring, which set a shaky tone for the rest of the term. The lectures are solid at explaining concepts, but the real-world examples felt thin, so I relied a lot on the recordings and notes on days I could barely squeeze in a session after work. The TAs were practical and quick to respond, which helped when I finally showed up for office hours to sanity-check a tricky password-cracking workflow we were asked to outline, though the grading comments took ages to land and sometimes felt more like a checklist than feedback on my actual approach. Instructions often left room for interpretation, which meant I spent extra time guessing what the rubric wanted, especially around risk assessment vs. mitigation. Time pressure was manageable most weeks, but the early confusion still shaped how I approached projects, and I ended the term barely passing after a term of grinding through short evening sessions.

Cyber Security Basics in the first semester felt like a rough climb that paid off more than I expected. The workload was heavy at times, but the material finally clicked once I started relying on the recordings and notes rather than fighting the live lectures, and the prerequisite gaps were surprisingly well addressed as the term went on. I barely scraped a pass after a term of struggle, yet I left with real momentum for the specialization, thanks mostly to office hours that saved me when I hit a wall with the tool stack. Grading comments came late but were detailed enough to guide me, and while I disliked the tension of the term, I learned a lot and appreciated how the software toolbox became manageable after a shaky start.

Taking Database Systems in my first semester was worth it for the specialization I’m chasing, since the relevance to data modeling and queries isn’t abstract at all, even if the pace feels ridiculous at times. I fell behind early while juggling another hard class, then somehow pulled it together right around the big project deadlines, which kept my mood hostage to the calendar more than the material. The peer discussion sessions helped a lot—some classmates explained indexing and normalization in a way the official lectures barely touched, and I clung to those chats when the tooling kept hiccuping at the worst moments. The project-heavy structure and the high-stakes exams are real, and the fast feedback on scores comes with explanations that are toothpick-thin, so you’re told what you got wrong but not always why. The platform timing failures made a couple of deadlines feel weeks longer than they were, which added a weird extra level of stress when I was trying to catch up. Overall I’d say it’s relevant and worth the grind, but you’re judging it against your expectations rather than another course, and the biggest memory is wrestling with the workflow more than the concepts themselves.

I’d say the course is a tough fit if you’re just trying to slot something into a busy schedule, and I only stuck with it because it lined up with other things I had going on. The lectures are a decent reference, but they feel dry and a bit lecture-y, so I relied on the recordings more than I expected. I fell behind and then caught up around deadlines, and even after the grade came in I’m still not sure how I felt about it—the outcome was not great, but I did pick up some basics, which was the point of me being new to the discipline. The rubric felt vague enough that I wasn’t sure what exactly counted, and the work was mostly solo, which didn’t help with motivation beyond ticking boxes. There was a small project around matrices that helped, but overall, I’m indifferent about whether I’d recommend it.
Linear Algebra was a mostly calm slog, but I learned a lot even when the vibes were rough. The peer discussions saved me near deadlines, though feedback came too late to fix my messy midterm prep.

I treated Computer Networks as my main focus this term, and while the organization kept things moving, the materials were rough—chopped notes, PDFs that lacked clear mappings to the lectures, and a lot of guesswork on what to study for the midterm. The timing of feedback felt sparse until it was too late, but office hours rescued me more than once; the sessions with the TA were the rare moment the course felt coherent.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Database Systems, but the workload often felt heavy for my limited study time since I’m juggling a full-time job. The tooling and setup took more effort than it seemed to pay off, and a lot of it felt tangential to grasping the concepts, even though the TAs were responsive and practical when I asked for help. The assessments were few but carried a lot of weight, so I spent more time polishing a single submission than I’d anticipated, and I’m not sure the final grade reflected my understanding as clearly as I hoped. The course fits best if you already have adjacent material under your belt, and I learned more from the practical bits than from the bigger structure of the lectures. Overall, Prof. Cohen kept things calm, and I appreciated that, even as I gave up a bit of sleep to keep pace.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Computer Networks with Dr. Park, and I’ll admit the ramp-up felt sharp after the accessible intro. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped when I had a rough mid-semester crunch and sporadic motivation. TAs were responsive and practical, and I felt supported enough to push through the tougher weeks, especially around the project deadlines. The course looks best if you have a study group, since collaborating kept the core ideas from drifting, but accessibility felt lacking at times—the material didn’t always land for me on my own. I’m in the failed tier with mixed feelings, still unsure if the effort was worth the payoff.

I’m not sure I’d recommend it, but I can’t shake how some parts stuck with me after late in the semester turned a corner. The course felt like an intro service class that gave you the basics in a rush, and I had enough time but my motivation was all over the place, so I used the materials here and there when I absolutely needed them rather than following a steady rhythm. The software stack started rough—setup dragged, and I remember a frustrating moment when the environment wouldn’t load the first time I tried a quick project—but once I got past that, it was still clunky, but workable enough to push through. Feedback varied a lot by assignment, which didn’t help my inconsistent momentum, and I’d say the course works a lot better if you’re in a study group to bounce ideas off; I relied on one friend to sanity-check my approach before the big task. There was a late-semester turning point I anchored on, where a project finally clicked, but I still left with mixed feelings after failing the course and wondering what the real takeaway was. The vibe was “some of this sticks, some of it feels like noise,” and I’m still unsure whether I’d tell someone to dive in.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty catching up this summer, and this OS course rubbed in a few realities I hadn't scheduled for—mostly the pace and the heavy deadline cadence. I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the practical part never clicked for me; slides passably clear but not memorable, and the emphasis on frequent assignments made it feel like I was chasing deadlines more than learning concepts. Tooling setup was a snag from week one, which sapped some motivation right when I was juggling full-time work, and most of the work ended up being solo rather than collaborative. The one standout moment was that surprise week where the exam felt like a relay—one memorable scramble, then a curve salvaged an A-ish result, but I still wouldn’t call it something I’d recommend, especially if you’re hoping for clear connections to real-world systems.

I took Database Systems with Dr. Park mainly out of curiosity, juggling a full-time job, so I appreciated the smooth LMS flow and the heavy deadline rhythm; the comments came later but were pretty detailed, and group study helped when the stack of assignments piled up.

Calculus II was an odd fit for my last semester before graduation, mainly because I took it to fit the schedule rather than out of pure interest. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and the deadlines sometimes blurred with session notes, so I fell behind and only caught up around a couple of key deadlines. Feedback comes fast enough to adjust, but the instructions leave too much interpretation, and by the time I realized the collaboration expectations were unclear, it was already crunch time. I learned a lot, but I still wouldn’t say I enjoyed the ride.

Taking Computer Networks as an advanced elective was a mixed bag: I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the material itself is solid, but the whole experience felt heavier than I expected. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, and for the most part the project-heavy workload lines up with the high-stakes exams, which helps me stay focused even when the concepts get abstract. Dr. Chen lectures briskly and the pacing does push you to stay on top of readings, though the prerequisite feel like it assumes more prior knowledge than advertised; I hit a few early weeks where I felt I was playing catch-up rather than building on what I knew. The feedback comes quickly—scores arrive fast—but the explanations are thin, which left me staring at the rubric and still not sure where I went wrong on certain choices. One concrete pain point was a late-September deadline where the project requirements shifted mid-iteration, and I had to redo a chunk of wiring between the network model and the test harness. Overall, the assessment felt fair but exhausting, and the course trades depth for breadth in a way that makes you sweat the whole semester, with a couple of practical wins toward the end that kept me going.

Cyber Security Basics was organized enough to feel manageable, but the platform quirks + the vague prerequisite jump left me frustrated, especially since I’m comfortable with proofs yet not heavy on system work; the few assessments actually mattered and arrived fast, though explanations were thin.

Summer term in Data Structures felt rushed but manageable; I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the workload was solidly positive. I liked the instructor, but grading comments came late and the examples were thin, which left me unsure about recommending it.

Calculus II with Dr. Park felt like I learned a lot, but the week-to-week pace in lectures was uneven and the whole thing didn’t click consistently. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, and I fit study around short evening sessions, which helped, though the feedback on assignments varied a lot in quality and felt inconsistent. The mix of assessments didn’t align with what was emphasized in lectures, and I left with a stronger coding intuition but weaker theory grounding. One small moment stuck, when a problem on my project graphing tool finally clicked after I watched a late-night recording and realized I’d been misinterpreting a limit step. Overall, the administrative side is fine, but communication could be sloppy.

I took Database Systems mainly because it was required for my degree, and Prof. Rios kept the lectures organized enough that I could follow along when I needed to and skim when I didn’t. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I relied on them selectively, especially when a reading puzzle clicked into place after I tinkered with a small ER-to-relational mapping exercise. Feedback came quickly enough to adjust before the next quiz, which helped, but the tooling side felt clunky—some of the ORM demos lagged and I ended up doing more hand-holding myself than I would have liked. A group project mattered more when our team actually coordinated, though it suffered a bit when teammates weren’t on the same page; I wouldn’t take it again, but it did build nicely on the stated prerequisites and the curve pushed my grade to an A. My memory anchor is a late-night forum thread and Prof. Rios’s quick office-hours response that finally clarified a confusing constraint.

Data Structures dragged along with my full-time job, and I mostly used the materials only when required. The pacing felt off, especially during a mid-semester crunch, and I’m not sure the grade reflected actual understanding; the project-heavy setup with little peer help didn’t help.

Taking Linear Algebra with Dr. Chen was a rough ride for someone new to the discipline; the material felt like a lot to absorb and the prerequisite fit wasn’t as forgiving as I hoped. The group work sometimes helped when teammates pulled their weight, but other times I felt left to scramble for clues while the deadlines stacked up unusually, and feedback usually arrived too late to actually fix what I was doing wrong. The course leaned heavily on reports and time-consuming writeups, which I can handle, but it was frustrating to see hints of what was expected only after a submission. I’d probably wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push me to stare down tough ideas and grind through the basics in a way that’s hard to ignore.

Machine Learning with Dr. Park was a required hurdle in my track, and I kept up with nearly every lecture even though I have a strong coding background but weaker theory, so I relied on practical bits more than proofs. The assessment design felt doable and fair enough once I got the hang of the first couple of weeks, especially the weekly programming tasks that leaned on actual code, which I appreciated. However, the platform kept glitching during deadlines, so some weeks felt scrambled and I had to scramble to resubmit, which tainted the momentum a bit. Feedback arrived fast enough on those tasks, but the explanations were thin—mostly surface notes like “good approach” without digging into what to change or why, which left me guessing in a few places. The grading rubric still seemed vague to me, like I wasn’t always sure what tie-breakers the TA used, though the core ideas were clear enough to guide my revisions. I remember one office-hours session where Park pointed out a misstep in feature scaling that finally clicked, a concrete moment that helped more than any long write-up would have. Overall I’d say the course ramps up sharply after the initial accessible start, and the practical focus helped me keep pace even while juggling another hard class.

I took Database Systems while juggling a full-time job, and the exam fairness left me doubtful—I felt tripped up by tricky questions that didn’t align with what we learned early in the course. The setup and tool work took age, and I spent more time debugging the environment than actually understanding the material, but I did manage to catch up around deadlines, especially when classmates formed a study group that helped. Overall, useful but not enjoyable, and I’d still say I’d recommend it to others who can keep pace.

Data Structures was a solid watchful step in the middle of this heavy semester: I took it mainly out of genuine curiosity about how things are stored and accessed, and the course kept that interest alive even as deadlines piled up. The LMS flow was smooth enough for submissions, but setting up tools was a bit of a pain, and feedback chats came with fast scores but thinner explanations—still, peer discussions saved me more than the official materials.

I took Database Systems in my first semester because I needed it for a specialization, and Dr. Singh’s slides were serviceable but not memorable. The mid‑semester crunch hit hard, and the grading comments finally arrived after a long wait, though they were detailed enough to be useful once they showed up. Office hours rescued the course for me, especially since the platform quirks added avoidable stress during quick homework runs. One exam week still sticks in my memory as the moment a tricky proof plus system quirks almost did me in.

Data Structures with Prof. Rios felt like a necessary grind more than an exciting ride. I came in comfortable with proofs but not with the systems side, so the course expectations leaned hard on a prior depth that wasn’t really advertised, which left me scrambling at times when the tooling suddenly became the bottleneck. The software stack is rough at first but manageable later, and I used the materials selectively when needed rather than binge-studying the whole thing; still, the platform’s quirks sometimes ate into my study time during busy weeks. Attendance was irregular for me, but I kept the slides as a serviceable reference—not memorable, just adequate, and I wish the lecture delivery carried more spark. The instruction left room for interpretation in places, which added a weird layer of friction when deadlines rolled in, especially since I treated it as the main focus course that term while juggling another hard class. One memorable moment was week 6’s project defense—barely scraping the rubric and hoping the examiner would fill the gaps. Overall I’m glad I stuck with it, even if the prerequisite fit felt overstated and the practice could’ve been tighter.

Linear Algebra in the summer term dragged a bit with the pacing, but the lectures were clear and Dr. Singh kept us on track most days, even as the deadlines piled up. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the course builds well on the stated prerequisites, though the report-heavy workload and some tool glitches stretched weeks. I remember office hours once when a data visualization assignment click finally clicked for me, but overall the platform hiccups and time pressure when I was also juggling another hard class left me frustrated and unsure about the grade.

I took Database Systems mostly because it fit my schedule rather than because I was dying to dive into the theory, and I had enough time but motivation waned inconsistently. The lecturer was solid, clear during lectures and responsive in office hours when I needed a rescue, even if the explanations in the quick feedback emails felt a bit thin. The course had few assessments, but each one mattered a lot, so I rode a tight curve; best to come in with solid adjacent material already in hand. I’m coming from a strong coding background, but the theoretical parts felt loose, and the prerequisite fit is definitely smoother if you already know some of the basics. Comparing it to easier prerequisites, this felt tougher, especially while juggling another hard class, and I’d hesitate to recommend it despite the value I did extract. The moments I remember most are those office-hour sessions where I finally clicked a concept, and that’s what saved the course for me.

The OS course is a mid‑semester grind, and I’m juggling it with two other tough classes, so I’m not surprised that I’m chasing the parts that actually clicked. I liked the instructor and the practical demos, but the grading felt like it didn’t quite track the effort I put in, especially compared to the easier prerequisite I survived last year. Group work can be helpful when the team actually splits tasks well, and our TAs were responsive enough to steer us back on track when we got stuck coding the process isolation part. The LMS flow stayed smooth, which saved a headache during deadline week, and I’ll admit I appreciated their quick fixes on small submission glitches my group hit around week six. Overall, it’s solid enough to keep marching through, even if some parts feel a bit clunky.

Operating Systems was a solid B for me, which matches the level of effort I poured in while juggling two other demanding courses in the final stretch before graduation. I mainly relied on recordings and notes, since the live lectures felt patchy and I preferred pacing myself around deadlines that sometimes clogged up weeks. The quick feedback helped me adjust, but tooling problems during deadline weeks turned a few tasks into a scramble. Instructions often felt a bit open to interpretation, which added some friction, yet group work could be valuable when the team clicked. One memory sticks: that tricky midterm week that hit right after a long project sprint, and somehow I kept my head above water.

I’m in my first semester and took Data Structures mainly out of curiosity, and I appreciated Prof. Cohen’s clear lectures and steady pacing. The course felt project-heavy with some high-stakes checks, and I found the prerequisites laid out well enough to build on; I relied on the materials selectively, mainly when the group helped me see a tricky graph problem. Overall, I liked the instructor but the grading left me unsure.
